CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
["There are one or two things which I deem it my duty to bring to the notice of the minister in connection with this Resolution and the Civil Service. In the first place, I think work is imposed on the Civil Service Commission that they should not be called upon to perform. The resolution seeks to appoint a body of men, not exceeding five in number, of whom four will receive $6,000 and one $7,000 a year. Such a body of men is almost equal in number to the membership of any of our Supreme Courts. Now we all know what important duties are discharged by a judge of the Supreme Court, and what important work the Supreme Court in any province, as a body, is supposed to perform. It would be very absurd if we were to appoint judges, with salaries ranging from $7,000 to $8,000, to do work that could well be performed by a justice of the peace. No Government could justify such a proceeding as that, yet it is exactly what is happening here. The appointment of a tide waiter in the county of Guysborough, the appointment of a fishery guardian in the county of Pictou, the appointment of a postmaster in the county of Victoria, which I have the ihoifour to represent, thousands and thousands of such appointments are being

made all over the country, and we have a commission sitting in Ottawa to whom we are to pay $31,000 a year in salaries alone, not 'to mention incidental expenses, to deal with matters oi that nature. 1 think such a proceeding is highly improper. I am entirely in favour of appointing big men to handle big questions; but I certainly do not approve of having a commission, whose members are paid large salaries, to deal with small matters that can be dealt with by the most ordinary individual in the country. I submit to the minister that he should cut down the volume of work which is imposed upon this commission. Let him remove the manifold appointments of a petty nature that the commission now have to deal with, and let the appointments be made in some other way. It transpired last night, during our questioning of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, that the hundreds and thousands of fishery guardians that must be appointed in this country within the next few months, are first recommended by the fishery overseer, and then the nominations are sent to Ottawa to be confirmed by the Civil Service Commission. Is that not a work of supererogation? Is not that taking up the time and energy of the Civil Service Commission to no good purpose? In such cases the commission must of necessity accept the recommendation of the overseer, and must trust him to nominate the right man. If he has done so, why not put the appointee in office at once, and thus cut down the enormous amount of petty work which now goes to the commission, and the dealing with which does not require any executive ability at all. I submit that ii this is done much unnecessary work on the part of the commission can be dispensed with. It is not fair to ask the Civil Service Commissioners to sit down in solemn form and to pass judgment as to who shall be tide waiter at Big Bras d'Or, or who shall be fishery guardian in British Columbia. All these appointments could be dealt within another way, and in a manner more expeditious and less expensive to the country. I certainly protest against increasing the number of Civil Service Commissioners from three to five in order to deal with matters of this kind. If the real questions that should engage the attention of big, capable, brainy, well paid men were cut down to the class of work that should be done, you will find that three men could do it just as well as five, and with less trouble.
There is another thing about these examinations. I suppose the Government
think they are conferring a favour upon any candidate for a position in the Civil Service whom they let in with an easy examination. I do not view it in that way.
I do not think that a worse service could be done any young man in this country than to set an examination by which he could get into a lower class at an age between 18 and 25. He gets in after a certain examination. He is there until the next stage of promotion arrives, five or six years afterwards, when the age for learning has passed, when the time for going to school has gone and he finds himself up against a stone wall. He never can pass any more examinations and he has to stay where he is or go back into the world to seek some other work. I submit to the minister that he should always have in view the admission of good men to the service who would be capable of development and promotion from one stage to another and that he would in the different classes pass such an educational examination in the very first instance as to qualify a person educationally for promotion in that class until he reaches the top.
I am not in favour of asking candidates for the Civil Service to pass a high examination in Greek, Latin, geometry, trigonometry, and all those difficult subjects. I am in favour of a good English, or French education. I want a man to be a good writer, a good speller, to have a good knowledge of the English or French language, and such general knowledge as would bring him to a standard perhaps equal to our grade 12 in our curriculum, or qualify him to pass a first class teacher's examination. You have a man of good common sense and fair practical education. Put him at the bottom if you like but qualify him once for all so that if he is ambitious and capable he may look forward to getting to the top. It is no friendship or favour to any person to give him an easy examination whereby he can get into the first grade. He spends some years there, he cannot go to school again, he cannot pass any further examination and he is blocked for the rest of his life. I wish the minister to keep that in view when dealing with the educational test. As I read the examination papers and the curriculum prescribed for Civil Service examinations, it appears to me that it is not a fair test. In some things it goes too high, and you require an examination on subjects that keep many good people out of the service. People get in by reason of their ability to pass these", 'tests who are not as good as those who would get in if the test were along the line that I have suggested.
My whole remarks come down to this: That too much small business is imposed on the commission. Hundreds of thousands of cases which come before the commission might be dealt with by a most ordinary officer at an ordinary salary, and my other point is that I think the educational test should receive more consideration and that it should be conducted in such a way that it would secure for the service the right kind of man and the right kind of woman.
Resolution reported, read the second time, and concurred in.']

The Montreal Gazette of this morning contains a special cable despatch from its London Correspondent which reads as follows:
London, May 25.-A contract has been signed between the Canadian and Grecian Govern-, ment for the supply of 25,000,000 tons of wheat to Greece to be transported in Greek tonnage by the London shipping firm of M. Emibiricos. Ten vessels of five thousand tons are en route, and during the summer months will mostly call at Montreal.
I would like to inquire from the Ministei of Finance (Sir Thomas White) or the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), how much of this statement is correct. It is quite apparent that it is not entirely correct inasmuch as it represents more wheat than we would have to export for three or four years. I think it is important that a statement should be made as to how much of this information is correct and whether it is the policy of the Government to give precedence to the sale of wheat rather than the products of wheat.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
Negotiations
have been proceeding for the disposal of some wheat to the Greek Government but we have no official intimation up to the present time that any contract has been signed. Pending any definite information on that subject, I am unable to give a reply of the character which my hon. friend (Mr. Robb) would desire. I may say, however, that the efforts, of the Government have been directed towards the exportation of wheat products in the form which he mentioned. It is not always possible, in negotiations that are being carried on,
to accomplish that to the fullest extent desired. I am not quite sure whether any portion of this is to go in the form of flour or whether the whole of it is to go in the form of wheat.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
I might add to what the Prime Minister has said that the amount involved is about a million bushels a month which will run to an aggregate of 12,000,000 bushels and cover a period of twelve months.
Sir .SAM HUGHES: May I ask how the prices are fixed in these deals?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
The price will
be the price in Canada at Port Arthur or Fort William, plus carrying charges to the seaboard and upon the ship. The Greek Government have been desirous of furnishing its people with the best possible flour, and they therefore desired to obtain a quantity of Canadian wheat. The matter was most carefully considered by the Government with those interested in the sale of our wheat, especially wheat of this year s crop, and it was thought desirable in the national interest that the wishes of the Greek Government should Ibe met, with the result that some twelve or fifteen million bushels of wheat will be sold. About three million bushels of that will be of this year's exportable surplus; the balance will be of the coming year's crop. I may say that the Government considered it desirable that no effort should be spared to furnish as far as possible a market for the entire exportable surplus of this year's wheat crop, including, of course, " wheat " flour, whioh is a product of wheat.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: If I may trespass again, does this apply to the raw material, or will the Greek Government take flour?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: This applies to wheat, because the Greek Government wants wheat. The policy of the Government, as I explained to my hon. friend when the deputation waited upon us not very long ago, has been, to the utmost extent possible, to promote the sale of Canadian wheat in the form of flour. But obviously it cannot all be exported in that form, and the Dominion Government would not feel justified in missing the advantage of a sale such as this, with its ultimate beneficial consequences, by reason of the fact that the Greek Government desires to make this purchase in the form of wheat.

That the provisions of the said Act relating to temporary employment, dismissals, resignations, hours of attendance, annual reports, regulations, examinations, classification, appointments, promotions, transfers and compensation be amended, and that provision be made for re-classifying the Civil Service and for any additional expense which may result from such re-classification.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: Last year when the Civil Service Commission was being appointed, the hon. member for Muskoka and myself took up with the Prime Minister the question of appointing a returned soldier as a member of the commission. speechtext:
On the same line as
the question put by my hon. friend, I suggested last year when the minister introduced his Bill that a woman should be
appointed to the commission; first of all in view of the large number of women who are in the Civil Service; and, second, in view of the fact that we have now given the suffrage to women. Under these circumstances they ought to be represented on that commission.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: What about my question?

speechtext:
I cannot answei
my hon. friend's question; I do not like to anticipate the action of the Government in the matter.

speechtext:
As to the principle,
does not my hon. friend see eye to eye with me?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
I assent to the
principle that women are entitled to the suffrage and to fill any position that they are capable of filling. I cannot say? however, whether I am in favour of the appointment of a woman to the Civil Service Commission and at the moment I do not propose to bind the Government or myself in that matter.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: Not even for the time being?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
This is a time
when the Government ought to practise economy. I do not see any reason why there should be an increase in the number of Commissioners. Commissioners when three are sufficient to do the work?

speechtext:
The principle oi
enlarging the commission may be right or may be wrong; it will be for Parliament to settle that question. At the present time the commission is an exceedingly busy organization and the view is.held by many that they cannot possibly do justice to the great volume of work that is before them from day to day. During the reconstruction period it may fairly be held that the commission should be enlarged by the addition of further members. The Bill will provide that the number will automatically revert to three. I will read the section which will appear in the Bill.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: I do not know whether the minister has already explained the reasons for the introduction of this resolution and of the Bill which is to be founded upon it. If he has not, would he be good enough to do so, and to state also whether it has anything to do with the reclassification that has been in progress for some months, so that we may understand what we are talking about?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: I propose, with the permission of the House, to advance this Order to-day to the extent of having the resolution adopted. I shall not move the first reading of the Bill to-day, because what are known as the classification schedules are not yet fully printed. I hope that some time during the next week they will be available and that when I move the first reading of the Bill I shall be able to place on the Table, and possibly in the hands of hon. members, the printed classification schedules. I do not wish, therefore, to make any extended explanation of the Bill this afternoon, if I can avoid doing so. However, I desire to say just a few words.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: So that the reclassification will be under discussion at the same time as the new Bill?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
Yes. Hon. gentlemen will remember that under the Civil Service Act of last year the commissioners were directed to reclassify the service. Since last August, experts employed by the commission have been engaged tin that work. As I have already stated in the House during this session, the task was a stupendous one; otherwise the reclassification would have been submitted to the House long before this. I assure hon. gentlemen that it involved a great deal of

work, but satisfactory progress. has been made and the work is about completed; in fact, the actual classification has been completed-the delay is in the printing. The classification involves the arrangement of the whole Civil Service, outside and inside, into classes. For instance, there is a clerical service, which will be common to a great many of the .departments; the felerical force is found in almost every department. To-day the clerical staff of the Department of Public Works, for instance, may be paid on an entirely different rating from that which applies to the clerical services in other departments. The scheme of reclassification will put all the clerical staff into one service; the members of that service will be paid according to their duties and responsibilities and there will be no variation in the salaries throughout Canada. The postal service is a service by itself, because everybody engaged in the postal work belongs to the postal service. There may, however, be a clerical staff in the post office which will become part of the clerical service.
I should like to give to the Committee a definition of some of the new terms which will be imported into the Bill ratifying the classification. The word " position," which will be used frequently, is understood to mean " one specific office or employment occupied normally by one person." For example, a man may have the position of delivering letters, or taking dictation, or driving an automobile; his position is defined.
The word " class " will be used also in the reclassification and in the amending Bill. " Class " is understood to include all those positions, employments, or offices the duties and responsibilities of whose incumbents and the qualifications required and demanded of applicants therefor are sufficiently alike to be given the same denomination or title. In the Department of Railways and Canals, the Department of Public Works and the Department of Marine and Fisheries we have persons engaged in marine work; regardless of the department they are employed in, they will come within the class of marine workers.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: Engineers the same way?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: There is an engineering division. " Service " is understood to mean an aggregation of classes having similar functions. For instance, all the clerical staff, wherever found, inside or outside, regardless of department, belong to the clerical service. The classification will disclose the following services.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
Before my hon. friend
proceeds, may I inquire what is the name and location of the firm that made the reclassification, what are the names of the classifiers, and are there any Canadians among them?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: The work of reclassification was carried on 'by the Civil Service Commission who employed certain people to do it. The principal assistants were furnished by the firm of Arthur Young and Company who are engaged solely in the work of classifying and organizing civil services.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: Of Chicago?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: Their main office is in Chicago, but they have offices in other large cities, including, I think, an office in Toronto. They furnished the Civil Service Commission with a certain number of experts and some Canadians were engaged in the work.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: What firm in Chicago would know about the working out of the Civil Service system of Canada?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: I do not see why a firm in Chicago would not be able to do the work just as well as a firm in Canada,

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: Then why not give the preference to a firm in Canada?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: I do not think there is in Canada any person or firm that has ever given any attention to this class of work.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: Are these people not accountants solely?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: No, they are not accountants. Their attention is devoted entirely to work of this character, and they are now being and have been employed by many States and cities of the United States of America.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: As a matter of fact, is it not true that the heads of the department did the work of re-classification?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: No, they had nothing to do with it other than to give information when asked for it.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: Was not Mr. P. D. Ross available for this work?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: His services were not sought by the commission.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: Who is Mr. P. D. Ross?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: What is the remuneration.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: I cannot inform the hon. member as to the exact remuneration.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: How much per day?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: I cannot give the information. The firm of Arthur Young and Company engaged by the Civil Service Commission, was a very able body of men who knew their work well, and it matters little to me what country they are citizens of so long as they are capable of doing this particular work. I think it will be found, when the whole matter is submitted to the House and thoroughly understood, that they were very capable men.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: What is the rate of paj of this American firm; how many are included in their staff, and how much is the staff paid ?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: I am sorry I cannot give my hon. friend that information to-day. I would hardly be expected to carry that around with me, because there is no particular reason why I should know it. This Parliament authorized the Civil Service Commission to carry on this work, and the commission secured the services of this firm without consulting the Government at all. I shall, however, later on inform the House as to the probable cost of this work.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: Have certain departmental officials found it necessary to revise the classifications made by this firm?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: That question might be answered " yes and no." When the report is fully completed, the Civil Service Commission and the experts who are assisting them, do not expect the report to be without error. There are 60,000 positions in Canada which are being classified, and the classification schedules will occupy between six and seven hundred pages. There will be some 1,600 or 1,700 classes of positions classified in the service, and it would be almost too much to expect that such work would be absolutely free from error; in fact, the commissioners would be well satisfied it they did not find greater error than from five to ten per cent. From time to time the commission have consulted different members of the Civil service, sometimes a deputy minister, sometimes another departmental official. This was necessary, and I have no doubt that, from time to time, they secured from such persons valuable information which would induce them to revise a preconceived idea as to classification of any particular service.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: All of this leads one to wonder whether a commission of experts composed of our own officials would not have done the work better than this imported commission.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: I am not of that view, and I am sorry I cannot agree with my hon. friend. We shall be in a better position to judge of that when the schedules are printed and in the hands of hon. members. My opinion is that when the report is studied it will be the judgment of hon. members that the work has been well done and that it will ultimately prove to be in the public interest.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: Without wishing to be too persistent about the gentlemen who came from Chicago to revise the whole Civil Service system, I should like to know who recommended them.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: The Civil Service *Commission obtained the services of these men. They went out looking for men capable of doing this work; they could not obtain such services in Canada, and they took the best means they could of obtaining the names of some concerns outside which might do the work.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: Then I understand the Civil Service Commission themselves, without the recommendation of anybody, engaged these accountants or others in the city of Chicago?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: That is true.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: Thus trading and trucking with the Yankees.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
It would be unsatisfactory to the Committee and also to myself if I were to endeavour this afternoon to give an explanation of the classification without the schedules before me. I hope, therefore, the Committee will he good enough to permit progress to be made with the resolution, and when I move the first reading of the Bill I purpose giving as full an explanation as possible.
I should like, however, to give an illustration of what classification means. For instance, I have in my hand what will be a page of the classification schedule. This contains three schedules, and to give the Committee an idea of what a schedule actually .means, I will read it. The schedules are headed " Junior Forward Sorter," " Bor Collectors," and " Postal Labourer." These are three positions in the postal service. It is the position which is classified,

and not the individual. The responsibilities and duties of the position are first set forth,

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: There is nothing new there.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
When I move the first reading of the Bill I 'think I shall be able to point out oases in the Canadian public service where men are receiving at least one hundred per 'cent more than they should for the class of work they are doing. In other cases civil servants are underpaid for the class of work they are doing. I have read this schedule merely to give hon. gentlemen an idea of what a classification schedule means. The duties of a Junior Forward Sorter are set forth as follows:
Examples: Facing and sorting letters for the cancelling machine and hand stamper; revising and tying sorted letters ; opening, closing, and labelling mail hags; checking amounts of postage on mail matter; sorting letters for forwarding in one or more easy frames; sorting newspapers for forwarding.
From this the incumbent of the office can see what are the duties of his position. Heretofore, the duties pertaining to positions in the public service have not been defined except in a very casual way, and have varied according to the departments.
The schedule also states the qualifications for the position, 'which in this case are as follows:
At least public school education; good physical condition and a good memory; quickness of hand and eye.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: Public school qualifications?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: For this particular position of Junior Forward 'Sorter, the intention hereafter, and this will be provided for in the Bill, is that candidates for positions in the Civil Service shall be examined merely in respect of the duties of the office which they are seeking, instead of undergoing a general examination on matters which really do not relate to the duties of the office.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
That is well enough in its way, but will there have to be another
examination in the case of promotion to a position requiring higher educational attainments?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
There would be another examination in .respect of the work to be done in the new position to which the man seeks 'to be .promoted. The schedule also sets forth the principal lines of promotion, so that a person on entering the service in any position may know

what lines of promotion are open to him. Of course, it does not follow that the official will necessarily be promoted, because promotion will depend upon his record and efficiency. It was the judgment of the Civil Service Commission, however, that the lines of promotion should be stated in the schedule so that the incumbent of any office might know what other positions in the public service he might aspire to.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: Did I understand the minister to say when speaking on the Post Office Department that some officials of that department were receiving one hundred per cent more than they should be receiving?	[DOT]

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: No, I did not say that.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: I think so.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
I am certain I did not say that. I said that if I deemed it necessary or wise to do so, I could indicate some positions in the public service of Canada where the incumbent was receiving one hundred per cent more for the work he performed than the work was worth. The principal lines of promotion for junior forward sorter are as follows:
To perform, under supervision, simple tasks in connection with the forwarding1 of mail in a large post office and other related work as assigned.
To: Forward Sorter, Directory Clerk, General Registration Clerk, Money Order Clerk, Registration Clerk, Registration and Money Order Clerk.
I think it is an excellent plan to have inserted in the schedules the principal lines of promotion open to anybody in the Civil Service. The schedule finally states the compensation, under monthly and annual heads. The commission have examined fairly well all the civil positions in the public service of this oountry, and have classified the duties 'and responsibilities and qualifications of each class of posi-. tions. I do not think it is necessary for me to give any more examples.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: Does the report of this new commission differ materially from the report of Sir George Murray?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: My recollection is that the report of Sir George Murray was a general report on the conditions in the Civil Service of Canada. This new report has to do entirely with the re-classification of the service.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: The Murray report was discarded, if I mistake not.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: Did I understand the minister to say that the classification has been completed?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: I am curious to know what the minister is going to do when the report of the Special Committee inquiring into the manning of the Civil Service is presented. As this new classification is going to be confirmed by an Act of Parliament, does it not seem to the minister, labour in vain for this Special Committee to be toiling every day reconstructing what has already been reconstructed? I would like to know what the minister thinks this Special Committee is doing, and what the result will be when their report is presented.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: I really cannot tell my hon. friend what I think the Committee is doing, because I am not a member of it, and I should not like to make a guess. The Committee were directed to inquire into the question of whether or not the service was overloaded, and not to make a classification of the service. The reference to the Special Committee was of a more general character. I do not think there will be any conflict whatever between the two reports.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: What have been the salaries of the commissioners up to this time?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: The Chairman $6,000, and the Commissioners $5,000.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
In view of the fact that there is now a Special Committee of this House investigating whether the service is overmanned, and the further fact that the service has now practically been reclassified, having regard also to conditions generally throughout the country and the dissatisfaction with a lot of appointments made,.on what ground do the commission justify the appointment of two other commissioners to undertake work ithat has already been done? The Special Committee may report in favour of reducing the number of civil servants. Upon what ground does the minister base his opinion that there is going to be a large increase in the Civil Service of this country in the next two years.1
lit seems to me that this is entirely uncalled for. Instead of increasing the salaries of these commissioners, if they are not satisfied and are not able to get along w;th a salary of five or six thousand dollars



a year, the Government might be able to get other very estimable gentlemen who would accept the position at the present remuneration. There are doubtless many returned men in Canada that are perfectly competent to fill these positions, and would be glad to accept a stipend of $5,000 a year.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
The salaries of
deputy ministers were recently fixed at $6,000, and it was felt that the members of the Civil Service Commission occupy a position in the service analogous to that of a deputy minister. Let me point out that the duties of the Civil Service Commission will not terminate because the reclassification has been completed. The members of that commission could not have carried out that re-classification because their time is fully occupied with other duties, and on the first reading of the Bill to amend the Civil Service Act I propose indicating to the House in some manner the many duties which they have to perform. During the last twelve months a tremendous amount of work has been placed upon the commission, and the putting under their administration of practically the whole Outside Service has imposed an enormous additional burden on them. Furthermore, after the re-classification is adopted by Parliament the service must be fitted into it, which will be no slight task; also the Civil Service Act of last session, directed a reorganization of the departments,, involving additional duties. Again the placing of returned men in public positions in this country means additional work for tire commission, because a preference is being extended to those men. With the permission of the House I will read a clause which will appear in the Bill covering this extension of the personnel of the commission.
There shall be a commission to be called the Civil Service Commission, consisting of not more than five members appointed by the Governor in Council: provided, however, that after the expiration of three years from the first day of April one thousand nine hundred and nineteen no person shall be appointed a commissioner until the number of members of the commission is reduced to less than three, and after such reduction the number of members of the commission shall not exceed three.
After the lapse of a few years the Civil Service Commission will be better organized than it is to-day; its staff will have more experience, and the public will have become accustomed to the new order of things.
Mr. 'LBMIEiUX: My hon. friend stated a moment ago that as a result of the re-classification referred to, many civil servants would get an increase in their salaries,
.	,	'
whilst others might, perhaps, in future face a decrease. Might I call the minister's attention to what has taken place lately in a large corporation? The Canadian Pacific Railway has of late re-classified the salaries of its officials from coast to coast. Under that re-classification not only has the company considered the salaries of the officials who are in active service, but it has also, according to my information, given a pro rata increase to those who have been superannuated, on the ground that the cost of living and the prevailing conditions apply to the latter class, just as much as those who are serving actively. I understand that there are very few-at least only a relatively small number-public servants who are now on the retired list, and enjoying superannuation. I would therefore ask if it is the intention of the Government in the re-classification which will be presented to the House by my hon. friend to include the former officials who have been superannuated? The additional expenditure which would he involved thereby would not be large in view of the smallness of their number, and there is some justice in the claim for consideration in their case, because with a reduced salary, resulting from their superannuation they also feel the stress of the times we are passing through.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: I might say that no person now in the public service holding a permanent position will suffer any diminution in salary during his or her lifetime, even if the position which he or she fills is re-classified.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: That is, re-classified at a lower salary?

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
Yes, at a lower salary. The same provision was contained in the Civil Service Acts of 1908 and 1918. Thp schedules will show a very substantial increase in salaries, though speaking generally the compensation is not based upon the actual conditions to-day

the salaries have been fixed just as if the cost of living was normal and the war had not occurred. During last year a -bonus was paid to a very large section	of	the	CivilService, and that is being continued; in fact,	the Committee	will	be	askedto vote a certain amount this afternoon to enable	the bonus t-o be	paid	for	April,May and	June of this year.	After the
amended Civil Service Act becomes law, and the salary schedule which accompanies it is adopted, it is proposed to present to Parliament a scheme for the payment of a bonus to civil servants which will meet

the prevailing conditions, but that will probably not take place until very late in the session. My hon. friend has suggested that a bonus should be given to those employees who have passed out of the Service and been pensioned. My hon. friend was good enough to mention this matter to me yesterday, and two other persons in Canada wrote me making the same suggestion, but I have not had an opportunity of placing the matter before my colleagues. The first thing to be done will be to ascertain what additional cost will be involved if the suggestion is carried out. I readily admit theTe is much force in the suggestion because the purchasing power of the pension which is paid to these former officials has fallen very much, and I shall 'be very glad to give consideration to it.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: I might give my hon. friend a concrete case. Take, for instance, the inspectors of customs who ten or fifteen years ago received a certain salary, and whose pensions, when they were superannuated, was based on that salary. Their successors in the Service '.lave, since their promotion, had the benefit of one or two increases, and will now get a further increase, so that when they in turn are superannuated they will receive a pension proportionate to their salary. On the other hand, the men whom they succeeded are receiving a smaller pension based on the salary paid years ago. It seems to me that it is only a matter of justice to grant recognition in the way suggested to these former public servants.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
I think that in dealing with the salaries of civil servants we have commenced at the wrong end, I suppose, on the principle embodied in the old saying, "To him who hath shall be given. '
Those who stood most in need of salary increases were t'he men at the bottom of the list, getting from $1,200 to $1,400 a year. On these salaries they have been forced to exist-you cannot call it live-owing to the increased cost of everything they have had to buy and they have found their salaries, with the bonus addition, hardly sufficient to keep their families and themselves in any kind of decency. These, in my judgment, are the members of the Civil Service who should receive the first consideration but those who have received the first consideration have been the deputy ministers and the chief clerks whose salaries were comparatively large. I say " comparatively large " when placed alongside the salaries of others in the service who are getting $900, $1,000 or $1,200 a year.
185J
I fail to see how the hon. member (Mr. Sinclair) can possibly arrive at the conclusion he expressed a moment ago that the members of the Civil Service Commission were quite sufficient to do the work. *He was at that time criticising the increase in the number to five members. We have any amount of evidence that the Civil Service Commission were not capable of doing the work which fell to their lot. What did they do? They handed their work over to sub-committees. Applications were received for a position and a sub-committee was appointed to make >a choice from amongst the applicants. That did not occur only once; it occurred many times, showing very clearly that the Civil Service Commission composed of three members could not cope with the amount of work 'that fell to them. If the Government are open to censure at all for increasing the Civil Service Commission that censure should come to them because they did not increase it sooner. I- would very much rather have, not three, not five, but a dozen members of the Civil Service Commission who were in some sense responsible to this Parliament than have a commission of three finding themselves unable to do the work devolving upon them and making selections of men who have been milking the Government ever since they were big enough to appreciate the possibility of obtaining assistance from the Government.
A very notable example of that is the editor of the Ottawa Evening Journal, Mr. P. D. Ross, who from 1896 to 1911 succeeded in obtaining for advertising between $9,000 and $10,000 out of the Government of the country, who, in the last six years, has obtained from '.this Government alone over $24,000 in advertising and who, in addition, has obtained something over $62,000 for the rent of a part of the premises which he built and which he occupies as a newspaper office. Here is a gentleman who has been called upon by the Civil Service Commission, I believe, on more than one occasion, to decide whether this person or that person was the proper one to appoint to a Civil Service position.

Was it because of his very minute knowledge of every one of these departments that he lias foeen chosen to act on a sub-committee to make appointments which should be made by the Civil Service Commission? Is that the kind of a disinterested man that we should have making these appointments? I am told, and I believe on good authority, that it was an understood thing that when this gentleman put up the building that he at present occupies and holds, and from which he issues his paper, the Government would rent or lease a part of it for Government offices. In that way he was investing his money in such a way as to have a sure thing, that in the course of a few years he would get back, in the form .of rental, the money he had expended in putting up the building. This is the type of man who has been selected to do the work, in the way of making appointments, which should be done by a Civil Service Commission responsible to this House. This is the gentleman who takes advantage of the fact that he owns a newspaper, to criticise very severely any member of this House who ventures to express an opinion different from his own in regard to the members of the House having a say in the appointments which are made in their constituencies.
I repeat, in the face of the facts which have been placed before this House again and again, that the Civil Service Commission have been entirely unable to cope with the amount of work which has been thrown on their hands. In view of the fact that they have appointed sub-committees to deal with hundreds of applications for positions in the Civil Service, and in view of the fact that we have had men who are not responsible to Parliament, or to anybody else, making selections of persons for appointment to the Civil Service, it is high time that we had an increase in the personnel of the Civil Service Commission, so that we will have some person who is responsible to Parliament for the appointments which are made.
I do not blame the Civil Service Commission for it but that situation has developed through the assinine policy of this House in placing upon the Civil Service Commission work which could be better performed in the public interest by the

men who are responsible to the people, the representatives of the people sitting in this House. It is an absolutely ridiculous and illogical situation that faces this Htouse and the country to-day thalt we as members of the House are to be held responsible to the people for appointments which are made not by members of the Civil Service Commission but by sub-committees appointed by the Civil Service Commission and responsible to no person in the country not even to the commission itself.
That is an absolutely ridiculous state of affairs against which I want to protest, just [DOT] as I also want to protest against the way in which salary increases have been made in the Civil Service. Are we to suppose-perhaps we can get some consolation from looking at it from this point of view-that the only officers affected in the city of Ottawa by the high cost of living are the deputy ministers of the various departments, the chairman and members of the Civil Service Commission, and the chief clerks? Is it to be presumed that the high cost of living does not affect those men getting from $1,200 to $1,400 and that therefore it is not necessary to deal with them?

My hon. friend criticised my proposal that the commission should be reduced from five to three or that it should remain as it is at present. I think that is a proper proposition. It depends altogether on what w'ork the Civil iService Commission are endeavouring to do. Are they conducting clerical work? Or are they making inquiries throughout the country as to who a man is, what stripe of politics he is, and whether he ought to be appointed over somebody else? Are they engaged in work of that kind? If, on the other hand, they are engaged like judges, in delivering decisions, as they should be engaged., they could do the work all right, and the clerical work these gen-

tlemen are doing could be performed by a clerical staff. I cannot see why five commissioners would be any better than three in doing work of that kind, because we want the combined judgment of the commission in arriving at decisions according to some definite principles. These men have got a great deal of work to do no doubt; but 1 fear they are doing work that somebody else might be carrying on at a very much lower cost. Therefore, I still want to register my protest against increasing the personnel of the commission. I think a commission of three would be more efficient, and with a sufficient staff such a commission, I submit, would be able to do the work better than five commissioners, with less confusion and with much greater satisfaction to the country .

That concrete case explains, Mr. Chairman, many of the events that have taken place since 1911. The purchasing of the press en masse by the powers that be is one of the deplorable conditions to-day in Canada, and if the people have no direction from an independent press, it is because the press has surrendered its independence into the hands of those powers. The statement was positively made in the House of Commons in 1912 that the Ottawa Free Press, although parading as a Liberal paper, was really the property of certain Tory financiers. It is not surprising, therefore, Mr. Chairman, that the Free Press should have defended all the shady transactions since, because the price has been mentioned by my hon. friend. Not satisfied with receiving job printing contracts from this Government, not satisfied with accepting positions on important commissions, the proprietor of that paper receives large amounts every year for rentals. How can you expect the public to respect the press of Canada in view of such a condition of affairs.

It seems to me that the time has come when this House has

to do one of two things, either take back into our own hands the responsibility of making all appointments, or make this commission proficient in every way. It is evident to members of Parliament who have had anything to do with appointments during the last year and a half that things have not been working too smoothly. I have been told by deputy ministers that the Civil Service Commission is practically using their staffs for the purpose of ferreting out information that could be got for the asking from any member of Parliament. If you are going to exclude the advice of members of this House in these matters the principle embodied in this Bill is correct: we must enlarge this commission to such an extent that the work can be carried on fairly and well. These commissioners should not act upon, I was going to say, half information; they should not act without being well informed as to the merits and demerits of all appointments. The minister stated that one of the reasons for increasing the number of commissioners was the fa^t that soldiers had been appointed to different offices throughout the country. I refer him to page 1026 of Hansard, where an answer to a question is quoted which states that out of 1,672 permanent appointments and 14,570 temporary appointments made last year, a total of 16,242, only 1,834 were given to returned men. I might go on and say what everybody knows: the appointments they did get were those at the very bottom of the list. A year ago the Prime Minister, in answer to a question, gave what was practically a promise lo the House that if this Commission was enlarged a returned man would be given an appointment on it. Considering the great unrest that prevails in Canada to-day, and having regard to the great service that the returned men are rendering to the country at this present hour, there is no doubt in my mind that the appointment of a returned soldier to the Civil Service Commission would do a great deal to quiet things down and would cause returned men throughout the country to feel that their interests will be properly looked after.

Any remarks which I make this afternoon I shall not direct against the minister ad hoc respecting the subject now under discussion; I shall rather direct them, generally speaking, to the Government which is responsible for the legislation we are now called upon to consider. The senior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) has perhaps borne greater burdens than the ordinary man could bear; he has occupied several positions with respect to different departments. This is accounted for partly by the fact that the Postmaster-General (Hon. Mr. Blondin) is not in this House. Then, a number of ministers went away and the hon. gentleman took their places while they were travelling. It seems incongruous to have called for the return of these ministers and not to have them here to give a word of explanation when such an important matter as this is before the Committee. I direct my remarks particularly to the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell). There has been, not only throughout the country but within the Civil Service, a great deal of unrest that might have been obviated had a proper course been adopted at the proper time. I speak now as a member representing a rural constituency, and with a very strong feeling that right and justice should prevail in the Civil Service as well as in all other classes of the community. Some years ago, when the bonus was spoken about, I offered a suggestion on the floor of the House that in view' of the increased cost of living

MACLEAN; If the hon. member purposes discussing the matter of bonus to the Civil Service, I might say that immediately after the committee disposes of this matter, I purpose taking up the vote in connection with the bonus so that my lien, friend will then be enabled to discuss this particular subject.

I was saying that when the question of the bonus came up, 1 suggested to the House that owing to the increased cost of living there should be an all round increase in the w'ages of the civil servants of this country sufficient to meet that increased cost, and that coupled with, that, a bonus should be given to put civil servants in a position to meet some of the back debts which they might have contracted owing to the insufficiency of their salaries and the constantly increasing cost of the articles they are obliged to purchase. The Government in its wisdom at the time gave a bonus to a certain class in the Service, namely, to those earning under $1,800, and nothing at all was received by the poor devil who might have been thirty or thirty-five years in the Service, as I know some of them had been, and who happened to have a salary of $2,000 with a large family to support and under greater obligations in many instances than the man earning $1,800. Had my suggestion been adopted at the time, the minister would have got rid of one of the great reasons of unrest in the Civil Service to-d'ay. The second reason for the present unrest in the Civil Service as well as the unrest throughout the country is the fact that the Government has taken no earnest steps to meet the profiteer. Whenever it was a case ot capital, well, capital had its way wdth the Government; but when it was a question of the ordinary consumer needing redress, then the Government was inactive or indolent or refused entirely to do anything. We have had one Minister of Labour who did his best according to his own light as minister of that department. He followed on exactly the same course as that on which the new Minister of Labour is following, but he was not considered to have had enough initiative or to have succeeded, and he was, therefore, set aside. We have now the same difficulties over again in an aggravated form

and the ministry-and I am not blaming my hon. friend, but I am blaming the ministry generally-have been indolent, inactive, and have not taken the proper steps to meet the increased cost of living and to keep down the undue profits that have been made in this country for some years past. It was mentioned to-day that there was a report by Sir George Murray, but the Government does not even know to-day what Sir George Murray's report was. There were reports from other commissioners, but the Government does not know what those reports were. There is a report now from some experts from the city of Chicago, and I want, as a Canadian, here and now to enter my protest against the action of the Civil Service Commission or the Government in going over to the United States to get a few accountants, or experts if you will, to do work in Canada that Canadians are quite competent to do. I do not think it is any arrogance upon my part to say that I have confidence that we have in Canada as good brains as those that are to be found in the country to the south of us. It is true there is a great deal of good and a great deal of money in the United States. It is true that from time to time it becomes necessary to go to the United States to borrow money. It is true that at times it becomes necessary to truck and trade with the Americans. All that is a business arrangement; but when we are told upon the floor of this House that in order to get brains enough to remodel the Civil Service, we have to go to the United States for them, I, as a Canadian, protest arid wish to make that protest as formal and as strong as I know how. The money has been paid for these men, and how much has been paid? When the Supplementary Estimates were under consideration, we were told that $46,650 were expended, and that is a pretty good pay for these American experts. Have they gone away yet? There are some cruel enough to say that after they have finished the re-classification of the deputy ministers, chief accountants and other high officials of the different departments, they are going to enter upon the gigantic work of reclassifying the Cabinet. I give that rumour for what it is worth; it may be true or it may not be true. If they are capable of classifying this Cabinet, it is no business nor concern of mine, but I wish them God speed, and I think they will have a difficult task before them. It is unfortunately the case in this country, and it may be so in 
many other countries, that when it is a question of paying a man a very high salary, that man's case immediately assumes such proportions that it must be considered at once; but when we, the poor men of Canada, who represent the poorer classes, the wage earners, the consumers of Canada, come before the Government, we cannot get from it that information, much less that action that we ask for.
What is the purport of this resolution which the minister pleads with us to pass, telling us not to consider for a moment the lack of information afforded, and that the information will be given at some later date? I accept the minister's word that the information will be given at some later date, but we are told that from time to time. We longed for the return of the ministers in order that unrest might be allayed in Canada, and what were we told yesterday: Wait one month for the report of the commission and then the Government will tell you what it will be able to do. While I do not want to charge the Government with not doing things they cannot do, and while I am with them in the upholding of law and order in this country, there is another way of settling the present unrest, and it is not necessary to wait another month. Action may be taken at once. Get after your profiteers; lower the cost of living, so that the wage-earner can keep his family and himself, and then you will settle all the unrest in this country. This is not a matter that has cropped up since the war ceased, nor did it begin during the war; we have been complaining of it ever since 1912. The Government knows that the cost of living has been increasing ever since that year. The Government was prepared for it, and they got together certain combinations to work out means. The Government threw aside the old Conservative party, and formed a new party, called the Unionist party. True and staunch Conservatives had to take back seats in order that the new blood which had been allied with other parties in the past could take the Teins in their hands and meet the situation. What has been the outcome of it all? A dismal failure, disunion in the Cabinet, assassination among the ranks; and that has contributed to the unrest in the Civil Service.

It occurred to me that the hon. Prime Minister was perhaps encumbered with the present number of his ministers. Journeys to Europe being now at an end, we have two Ministers of Militia, and the position of commissioner might be deemed suitable for one of them or perhaps for the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), as a reward due to the services he has rendered the Union Government, as all the ministers have now returned and there no longer exists a vacancy.
