While I have no desire to advocate strikes, I may say it is quite natural for those who get inadequate salaries to be dissatisfied and to try in every way to better themselves.
Conditions are very serious to-day and I must protest against the inaction of the Government who do nothing at all for the consumers and who, since they are in power, speaking not only of the present Administration but also of the former, since 1911. have exclusively concerned themselves about the millionaires and the manufacturers, without doing anything for the people.
Why should they be so solicitous of commissioners who are earning $5,000 or $6,000 a year? Why should they be so concerned about deputy ministers who are getting $5,000 or $6,000 in salaries, when they do not care at all for the men who only receive $50 or $75 a month?
Mr. Chairman, when we have to pay such high prices as we are now paying for food, when we have to give 75 cents a pound for butter and $10 for a pair of shoes, and when the Government give but $50 a month to some of those employees, it is the Government, I say, who are responsible for all those evils and I cannot blame the men who go on strike under such circumstances.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext: I am very much obliged to my hon. friend for his references to myself; I appreciate them very much. I can assure the hon. gentleman that the salary schedules which relate to the lower positions in the Civil Service will show a marked increase over the existing rates, and the bonus which must be given this year will,, of course, add to that. I would like to impress upon the hon. gentleman, and upon every member of the House, that all people in the Civil Service cannot receive the same compensation because their responsibilities and duties differ. I know of no other principle upon which any body can be employed 'and paid than according to the nature of the responsibilities that are assumed and the duties that are discharged. Unfortunately it may happen at times that those in the lower positions in the public service are unable to get a salary which perhaps may be deemed suitable, having regard to adverse or unfavourable conditions which affect the cost of living. That is to be regretted, but it is applicable to all other classes of work as well as Government activities. However, I hope when the bon. gentleman sees that classification schedule he will be pleased with the compensation 'to be given to those in the lower ranks of the public service.

maintopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN CANADA AND GREECE FOR SUPPLY OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
There are one or two things which I deem it my duty to bring to the notice of the minister in connection with this Resolution and the Civil Service. In the first place, I think work is imposed on the Civil Service Commission that they should not be called upon to perform. The resolution seeks to appoint a body of men, not exceeding five in number, of whom four will receive $6,000 and one $7,000 a year. Such a body of men is almost equal in number to the membership of any of our Supreme Courts. Now we all know what important duties are discharged by a judge of the Supreme Court, and what important work the Supreme Court in any province, as a body, is supposed to perform. It would be very absurd if we were to appoint judges, with salaries ranging from $7,000 to $8,000, to do work that could well be performed by a justice of the peace. No Government could justify such a proceeding as that, yet it is exactly what is happening here. The appointment of a tide waiter in the county of Guysborough, the appointment of a fishery guardian in the county of Pictou, the appointment of a postmaster in the county of Victoria, which I have the ihoifour to represent, thousands and thousands of such appointments are being

made all over the country, and we have a commission sitting in Ottawa to whom we are to pay $31,000 a year in salaries alone, not 'to mention incidental expenses, to deal with matters oi that nature. 1 think such a proceeding is highly improper. I am entirely in favour of appointing big men to handle big questions; but I certainly do not approve of having a commission, whose members are paid large salaries, to deal with small matters that can be dealt with by the most ordinary individual in the country. I submit to the minister that he should cut down the volume of work which is imposed upon this commission. Let him remove the manifold appointments of a petty nature that the commission now have to deal with, and let the appointments be made in some other way. It transpired last night, during our questioning of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, that the hundreds and thousands of fishery guardians that must be appointed in this country within the next few months, are first recommended by the fishery overseer, and then the nominations are sent to Ottawa to be confirmed by the Civil Service Commission. Is that not a work of supererogation? Is not that taking up the time and energy of the Civil Service Commission to no good purpose? In such cases the commission must of necessity accept the recommendation of the overseer, and must trust him to nominate the right man. If he has done so, why not put the appointee in office at once, and thus cut down the enormous amount of petty work which now goes to the commission, and the dealing with which does not require any executive ability at all. I submit that ii this is done much unnecessary work on the part of the commission can be dispensed with. It is not fair to ask the Civil Service Commissioners to sit down in solemn form and to pass judgment as to who shall be tide waiter at Big Bras d'Or, or who shall be fishery guardian in British Columbia. All these appointments could be dealt within another way, and in a manner more expeditious and less expensive to the country. I certainly protest against increasing the number of Civil Service Commissioners from three to five in order to deal with matters of this kind. If the real questions that should engage the attention of big, capable, brainy, well paid men were cut down to the class of work that should be done, you will find that three men could do it just as well as five, and with less trouble.
There is another thing about these examinations. I suppose the Government
think they are conferring a favour upon any candidate for a position in the Civil Service whom they let in with an easy examination. I do not view it in that way.
I do not think that a worse service could be done any young man in this country than to set an examination by which he could get into a lower class at an age between 18 and 25. He gets in after a certain examination. He is there until the next stage of promotion arrives, five or six years afterwards, when the age for learning has passed, when the time for going to school has gone and he finds himself up against a stone wall. He never can pass any more examinations and he has to stay where he is or go back into the world to seek some other work. I submit to the minister that he should always have in view the admission of good men to the service who would be capable of development and promotion from one stage to another and that he would in the different classes pass such an educational examination in the very first instance as to qualify a person educationally for promotion in that class until he reaches the top.
I am not in favour of asking candidates for the Civil Service to pass a high examination in Greek, Latin, geometry, trigonometry, and all those difficult subjects. I am in favour of a good English, or French education. I want a man to be a good writer, a good speller, to have a good knowledge of the English or French language, and such general knowledge as would bring him to a standard perhaps equal to our grade 12 in our curriculum, or qualify him to pass a first class teacher's examination. You have a man of good common sense and fair practical education. Put him at the bottom if you like but qualify him once for all so that if he is ambitious and capable he may look forward to getting to the top. It is no friendship or favour to any person to give him an easy examination whereby he can get into the first grade. He spends some years there, he cannot go to school again, he cannot pass any further examination and he is blocked for the rest of his life. I wish the minister to keep that in view when dealing with the educational test. As I read the examination papers and the curriculum prescribed for Civil Service examinations, it appears to me that it is not a fair test. In some things it goes too high, and you require an examination on subjects that keep many good people out of the service. People get in by reason of their ability to pass these

tests who are not as good as those who would get in if the test were along the line that I have suggested.
My whole remarks come down to this: That too much small business is imposed on the commission. Hundreds of thousands of cases which come before the commission might be dealt with by a most ordinary officer at an ordinary salary, and my other point is that I think the educational test should receive more consideration and that it should be conducted in such a way that it would secure for the service the right kind of man and the right kind of woman.
Resolution reported, read the second time, and concurred in.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.

speechtext:
*On the motion of Hon. Mr. Rowell the House went into Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in'the Chair.
To provide for the continuance of the payment to those employees of the Civil Service to whom a War Ronusi (including: provisional allowance under item 419 voted at the last Session of Parliament) was authorized to be paid under the provisions of the Order in Council dated the tenth day of December, 1918, and the Orders in Council incorporated therewith, or in amendment thereof, and who are still in the Service, of amounts equal to one-fourth of the amounts so authorized to toe paid to them during the fiscal year 1918-19, toy way of a War Bonus for the first quarter of the fiscal year 1919-20, $2,500,000.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: Will you kindly explain that?

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen no doubt are acquainted with the fact that last year a war bonus was granted to the Outside Service and also to members of the Inside Service. The bonus was first granted to the employees in the postal service, I think in September last, but it was not made applicable to those who were receiving a salary in excess of $1,800. Later, the bonus was extended to large numbers of the Inside Civil Service, but again it was not made applicable to those who were in receipt of a salary of over $1,800. It was deemed advisable .and necessary to continue this bonus during the present year as conditions affecting the cost of living had not changed any since last year. It was not desirable to vote this sum of money by Order in Council-hon. members opposite, I am sure, will approve of that-but it was thought better we should come to Parliament and ask for a special sum to carry on this bonus as it was paid last year for the months of April, May, and June.
fMr. McKenzie.]

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: Will it stop then?

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: No, that is not the idea of the Government. As hon. members are aware there were many qualifications and limitations last year as to payment of the amount and its receipt by members of the -Service. It was thought that there were some inequalities and, perhaps injustices, in the method used in this regard. The Government accordingly submitted the whole matter to the Civil Service Commission, and we are hoping for a report from it shortly. In the meantime we wish the bonus to be paid as it was last year. Towards the end of June we hope 'to make a new submission to Parliament and ask for a larger vote. This now merely carries the bonus on for three months.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: In the constituency which I have the honour fo represent there is an experimental farm. I am informed by the labourers on that farm that the men higher up, the superintendent and the foremen, have received a bonus, but that the ordinary working men have not. If that is the policy the Government is going to pursue this year, I wish to register my protest against it.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: There are many persons in the employ of the Government who receive a daily wage, which in most places is at the market rate. For instance, in the city of Ottawa there are many classes of employees, tradesmen of one kind and another, who receive the market rate of wages. The bonus did not apply to that class, because it was thought they were receiving what was the current market rate for their labour. I assume that upon the same principle, possibly, these persons to whom my hon. friend refers did not receive the bonus. It may be that thev are not receiving a fair wage. If so, that should be investigated. I shall be very glad to discuss the matter with the Minister of Agriculture and later advise my hon. friend privately or in the House, just exactly what is the position.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext:
May I supplement what my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce has said? The matter is dealt with by Order in Council of the 10th day of December, 1918, in this form:
All persons known, as mechanical or labouring men employed at a yearly or monthly salary or wage shall toe entitled to receive the bonus. All those employed at a daily wage at current rates of pay shall not toe entitled to receive the bonus. All those .employed at a daily wage at less than current rates shall be entitled to

receive such bonus within the limits defined by the said Order in Council of November 7, 1918, and this report as the minister In charge of the department fn which such person is employed may recommend and the Governor in Council approve.
My hon. friend will see that the object was that where any men were employed by the day at less than the current rate of
wages-

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext:
Who is to define
what is the current rate?

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: Are those men on the permanent list or not?

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext:
They are not regarded as permanent employees of the department, although many of them continue in the public service for a long time. This is the principle involved: It was assumed that the classes referred to in the portion of the Order in Council just read by the President of the Council had received increased pay by reason of war conditions, and in that way had received their bonus. Now it might happen in case of the employees of the experimental farm in the eastern part of Quebec that they were overlooked entirely, and perhaps their pay was not increased at all, which of course would be unfair.
Mr. MORPHY': I would like to call the attention of the minister to the same thing that I have always complained about in this House, namely, that there is nobody to look after these men. They are not acquainted with the Orders in Council, they do not know whether they are permanent employees or not, and they are standing back too frightened to ask. When the-miniter says they get an increase in wages in accordance with the increase caused by the war, he forgets entirely the increased cost of living of these wage-earners, wdio have to work daily year in and year out as if they were permanent employees, but are not so treated. I repeat again-.and I hope the minister wdll take it into consideration-just	what I Said the other night
that it is the easiest thing in this House for a man who is getting a salary of $4,500 to have it raised suddenly to $6,000-a jump of $1,500-as happened in the Estimates under discussion at the time; while these
poor men all over the Dominion, in Ottawa and outside of it, with families to maintain, notwithstanding the increased cost of living are working along at $600 a year. I do not think that any able-bodied employee of the Government with a wife and family to support should be asked to w'ork for this Government or anybody else at $600 a year. It is about time that the Government realized that it is their duty to look into the lower branches of the Service through some specially appointed person, whose duty it will be to ferret out injustices and to remedy them.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: At the outbreak of the war certain civil servants joined the forces and were given their regular pay, in addition to which they received their pay as officers in the army, and, if they were married, their families received separation allowances. In many cases those men never went to France; some got safety-first jobs in England and others got safety-first jobs in Canada. Is it the policy of the Government, in addition, to favour those men with a bonus, while employees, as represented by my hon. friend from Kamouraska, are given no bonus whatever?

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: Civil servants who receive both civil and military pay are not entitled to the bonus under the Order in Council or under this vote.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: Nor do they receive separation allowances at all.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: Civil servants for whom I have a great deal of sympathy are the Dominion Police. They are a highly respectable body of men and have rendered, during.the last few years, most important services to Canada. I understand that last year they did not receive the bonus. I do not think it is fair that they should be overlooked; in my opinion they should be treated just the same as other public servants.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: My hon. friend perhaps will correct me if I am in error, but my impression is that the Dominion Police are not civil servants. They are under the Department of Justice. The fact that they are not civil servants would, I assume, be the reason why they do not come under this Order in Council. It would be quite a legitimate matter for discussion whether they should not receive some additional compensation.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext:
The Dominion Police are as much entitled to a bonus as office employees, day labourers, and others. They

are subjected to examinations; they are men of character and ability, and it seems to me that they are entitled to the same treatment as that which is accorded to other members of the public service.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: I wish to support the argument of my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) with regard to the Dominion Police. I cannot see any distinction in this matter between a member of the Dominion Police and a Public Works employee in Ottawa. Labourers in the Public Works Department have received this bonus. There is no real distinction between the permanency of a member of the Dominion Police and the permanency of a labourer in the Public Works Department. Moreover, the Dominion Police are not, I understand, paid as well as the City Police Force in Ottawa, and they have not the same advantages. They have not the superannuation, and many other privileges and advantages that the City Police Force have are not enjoyed by the Dominion Police. Therefore I strongly support the contention of the member for Maisonneuve that the Dominion Police should get the benefit of this bonus.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: I concur in what has been said with regard to the Dominion Police. They should be put in the same position as any other members of the public service who receive the bonus. They render efficient service, and are entitled to every consideration.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: I am under the impression that the question of a bonus or of increased compensation to the Dominion Police is under advisement by the Department of Justice. I cannot speak with certainty in the absence of the acting minister, but he will be here in a day or two, and I will bring the matter to his attention.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: Will my hon. friend attend to that? The minister is away, and the acting minister is away, too.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: The acting minister will be here to-morrow, and I will bring the matter to his attention.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext:
I wish to direct the attention of the minister to two other classes of civil employees who have not as yet obtained any bonus. I do not know about the employees of the Dominion arsenal at Lindsay, but I do know about those at Quebec. They are employed by the hour, the rate being fifty or fifty-five cents an hour for, mechanics. They have carried on during the war; they have done good work, but they appear to have had very little,

if any, wage increase during the war, and they have not been brought under the operation of this bonus. Another class which is, perhaps, even more deserving, comprises certain men employed in the Marine Department. Up to August, 1918, the employees of the Marine Department in Quebec had not received an increase of salary for ten or fifteen years. They were working at a great deal below current rates of pay, so much so that the Marine Department, which is not usually very generous in these matters, were finally obliged to grant them a very small increase. ,1 went into the matter thoroughly with ,the department at (the time and found that mechanics, boiler-makers and so on, in the Marine Department at Quebec were earning .about two-thirds of what men doing similar work were earning outside. These employees should be brought under the operation of the Order in Council which deals with the bonus. Furthermore, I cannot understand why a day labourer, as such, should not obtain a bonus while a salaried .man does. Of course, il see the viewpoint of the minister: That the wages of day .labourers have increased-

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext:
Especially where
they are organized, and in cities.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: Whether they are organized or not, their wages certainly have not increased in the city of Quebec. Owing to the benevolent attitude of the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries an attempt at organization on the part of the labourers in the Marine Department in Quebec city was so well squelched that not one of the .men has been able to return to his position. ,1 am afraid therefore, that the argument about organization does not go very far. As organization is impossible under a Government department in Q.udbec-although it seems to be quite possible elsewhere- these men should be given an adequate bonus and be treated the same as other employees in the public service have been treated.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext:
I have seen Estimates go through providing for increases of $500 and $1,000 respectively to deputy ministers and other officials. As a matter of fact, we are passing Estimates daily increasing the salaries of almost all employees the Government has, from deputy ministers down. Let me put in a plea for the man who is the most deserving of all the employees of the Government so far as increased pay is concerned, and that is the man who delivers the rural mail throughout the different parts of the country. For instance,

one rural mail courier whose route is about twenty-five miles long, gets $750 a year. His contract calls for the supplying of a horse and rig and of two horses when the roads are bad, and he has to furnish these horses and maintain them and his rigs, at that handsome wage. When we are giving additional pay to employees of the Government-in some cases where they have not asked for it-we should consider the case of these men. They are held down to their contracts and in imany cases they are working for starvation wages. The action of the minister would meet with general approval if he would give some assurance that an additional allowance will be made to the men who have signed contracts .to deliver mail in all kinds of weather for the paltry sums which they are receiving.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext:
I have been speaking to the President of the Council and to my hon. friend (Mir. A. K. Maclean) about the matter of giving consideration to a certain class of men who are employed in this building.
I have listened to the President of the Council (Air. Rowell) reading the Order in Council and the regulations under which those increases are made. He speaks of the current rate of wages, but it is hard to determine the current rate of wages. If the pay of any member of this House was to be measured by the current rate of wages out in the street, his pay might be cut down materially, and I suppose the man who is working at a carpenter job or digging a drain or anything like that, would be much better off than any of the members.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: A bonus was not withheld from the Parliamentary staff upon the ground set forth in that part of the Order in Council read by my colleague. The Order in Council provided that the bonus should be paid only to those who were employed during the whole year, and I think that pretty nearly every person whom my hon. friend has in mind is merely a sessional employee. It was under another part of the Order in Council that they were denied the bonus.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext:
I would be very brief if the minister would give me some hope that those men would be considered. Their salaries have not been increased; indeed nothing has been done for them. If he would increase their pay in some way, I do not care whether he calls it a bonus or not, it would be of great assistance to them. There are men in this class that I speak of who are bookkeepers; some of them have
charge of many men and are doing particular work, and yet they have not received any increase. Some of them come here from long distances and while they used to get a free ticket to come here, they have now to pay their way, and the cost of living has no doubt increased their expenses when they have come here.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext:
Have they had
any increases in recent years?

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: No increase whatever. I have had a talk with one of them who has been here for nearly twenty years and who is getting exactly the same pay as he was receiving twenty years ago. I do not care whether you call it a bonus or an increase of pay or an indemnity, the only thing I am after is that those men who come here from year to year, who, by reason of their coming here, have been to some extent disqualified for any other kind of work, who like to come here and who must come here to keep things going, should not be singled out and told that when others are receiving advances they must remain in the same old rut. I have spoken about this matter several times before, and I hope that the case of these men will be considered.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext:
I understood the
minister to say that the Government were considering giving a higher bonus, and I should like it to be made clear that they are also considering providing a bonus to Civil Servants who are receiving more than $1,800 a year. I can see no reason why the Government should fix this arbitrary maximum of $1,800 and stop there. A short time ago the Government and the House adopted a principle that shows conclusively that the bonus should not stop at $1,800. When they gave an increase to deputy ministers, they recognized the principle that a man who received more than $1,800 a year might be so affected by the increased cost of living as to require extra remuneration. I know of several cases of men who are receiving more than $1,800 a year and who are not able, upon the salaries they are receiving at present, to keep themselves and their families in the condition in which they are entitled to live. The cost of living to them has increased in proportion to the way in which it has increased to men earning less than $1,800 a year, and I hope the Government will consider the advisability of extending the bonus to men receiving more than $1,800.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext:
Has the Government given any consideration to placing in the class of Civil Servants those country and

village postmasters who have to devote all their time to the duties of office? I do not mean those postmasters where the post office is a side line. In my county I presume there would not he more than two or three of the class to which I refer and they should be classified along with the regular Civil Servants.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext:
They have not
been up to date, but the classification will show a division of all postmasters of Canada into ten ranks. In some cases this does not mean an increase in salary, for rural post offices, but it will affect the compensation. I might say in reply to the hon. member for New Westminster (Air. McQuarrie) that members of the Civil Service receiving an income in excess of $1,800 have placed before the Government what they deem to be their grievance by reason of the withholding of the bonus from them and the matter is now under consideration, non. gentlemen will understand that until the re-classification of the Service is settled and the salaries for the current year determined, it is difficult to decide what bonus should be paid, because the re-classification will place some men in a more favourable position than they were in before. Shortly after the re-classification is submitted to Parliament, we should be in a position to announce our policy respecting the whole service.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext:
I wish to draw the attention of the minister to the case of postal employees in the West. I refer particularly to most of the employees in the Strathoona post office which is a semi-staff office. These men have an initial salary of $600 per annum and with the temporary bonus and some olther living allowance which is [given to [DOT] them, their salary is brought up to between $900 and $1,000. The point on which these men have a grievance is that the ordinary mail carrier who does not require the same amount of clerical ability is drawing more money than the postal employees in the office. Under the present strike conditions prevailing throughout Western (Canada, these men have remained loyal to the service inasmuch as they have not gone out on strike, and last year when the Winnipeg and Calgary officers went out on strike, these men remained on duty in spite of the fact that they felt they had a distinct grievance and that it was not being looked after by the department. This method of granting an initial salary of $600 a year which must be supplemented by bonuses and living allow-

ances is peculiar, and I hope the minister will assure me that in the re-classification all these anomalies will be wiped out, and that the salary will be fixed, so that a man will know definitely what his salary is, and that if he is getting $600 or $1,100 a year that amount will not be reduced by the stoppage of any bonus, living allowance or any subterfuge of that kind. I gathered, and I hope correctly, from what the minister said, that in the re-classification provision will be made for the adjustment of cases such as I have mentioned.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext:
The minimum salary of the postal clerks at the present time is $600, and a living allowance of $180 has been paid for many years. There is also a war bonus, which brings the minimum up to $1,080. The maximum is $1,880, which is very much higher than the maximum of the letter carriers. The re-classi-fioation will fix the minimum and the maximum salary, and will provide for a bonus due to the high cost of living.
In answer to my hon. friend (Mr. Mc-Coig), provision has been made whereby if a rural mail contractor thinks his contract is at too low a price, he may ask to have it reconsidered and new tenders called for. We passed an Estimate the other evening for $375,000 to meet the increased cost to the country due to new tenders having been called from parties under the old contract.
With respect to the matter to which the leader of the Opposition drew my attention, namely, where contractors are held to their contract if no new tenders are submitted, I am looking into that matter; I think it should be remedied.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: Has any provision been made for fixing a minimum rate per mile for the rural mail couriers?

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: What was the amount of the bonus paid during the last fiscal year?

subtopic: VOTE TO PROVIDE A BONUS FOR CERTAIN CIVIL SERVANTS.
speechtext: It would approximate $800,000 per month.

speechtext:
I wish to protest against the habit we are falling into of granting increases without due consideration of where we are likely to land as a result. First of all, I do not like the term "war bonus" in this item; I do not think

there is any justification for it. I believe that where competition prevails you will get much better service, and I think that the feeling of unrest throughout the country today is in no small measure attributable to the action of Governments in this country in fixing the hours of work and the wages in the Service. Once people get into the Civil Service they receive so much in, I fear, many instances regardless of the service they render. There is no competition. In the case of the rural mail couriers, however, who tender for contracts, and where competition prevails, the lowest tender is accepted even if the sum is only half what another civil servant is getting who is not rendering anything like as great service. In view of the fact that a commission is now inquiring into the relations between employers and employees in Canada, I think this item should stand until we know the findings of that commission. The Government of this country, not this or the preceding Government, but all governments are responsible for fixing the hours [DOT]of labour in the service, which I believe are from six to seven hours per day. I believe the fact that men and women in the Service 'do not have to work more than six or 'seven hours a day is largely responsible for the unrest that prevails in Canada to-day, and which is in no small measure responsible for the high cost of living. The short day attracts people to the Civil Service. The real creators of wealth in this country, the people who are producing food, are also attracted to the city and the Service by the short day and once they get in the Service they think all they have to do is to hold a gun to the head of the Government to get anything they want. There is no 'reason why a civil servant should not leave the Service if he or she can better themselves outside, and I think the t:me has 'come when we should quit coddling civil 'servants. We should deal with them as 'other people are dealt with, as though we expected them to render value for the salaries received. I know the Government is in a very difficult position in dealing with these people, but I think the time has come for 'plain speaking, and -we might just as well *face the issue now as at any time in the future.

Before taking up clause 34, I would like to revert to clause 325. I understand that an amendment has been made to this clause as it originally stood, a fact of which I only learned yesterday, having, unfortunately, been absent from the House owing to indisposition.

the hon. gentleman is out of order in discussing the clause referred to, which has been adopted in his absence. The hon. gentleman, however, can by unanimous consent take the opinion of the Committee on a motion that the clause be reconsidered.

If you will permit me I would like to do that a little later on. The hon. member for Lanlbton (Mr. Armstrong) is desirous of speaking to the clause which has been called, but I would like if I might be permitted to move later on to reconsider clause 325.

I object to the
clause being reconsidered. A deputation from the city of Hamilton was heard in regard to it, and after a full discussion the Committee unanimously passed the clause in its present form. I for one object to the subject being re-opened.

I have no apology to offer for moving an amendment to this clause. It is true that in the early stages of the session I gave notice of a Bill which was worded similarly to this amendment. It is also true that the amendment went before the special committee appointed to consider this Bill and was defeated by a . small majority. Nevertheless, I believe that what I propose is in the public interest, and I hope the Committee will insist upon its being placed upon the statute book at the earliest possible moment, in order that the conditions which have existed in past years may not continue in the years to come.



The amendment I [DOT] propose is not as far-reaching as the one that was submitted to the special committee, and for this reason I laid it before Sir Henry Drayton, Chairman of the Board of Bailway Commissioners, and asked him to eliminate from it the words " in regard to ocean borne traffic." I also asked him to re-construct clause 358 of the Bill so as to confer upon the Bailway Commission control over the maximum rates to be charged; that is to say, that the commission should not have control over any other rates than the maximum rates. Sir Henry Drayton was good enough to re-draft the amendments in accordance with my wishes and I will submit them to the Committee. Sir Henry Drayton's letter to me on the subject is as follows :-
Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada. Office of The Chief Commissioner.
Ottawa, May 23, 1919.
Re Water borne traffic.
Dear Mr. Armstrong,-
You ask me to consider the amendments submitted, which read as follows:-
" Privilege and Concession to be under control of Board'.
" (A) 1. With respect to any privilege or concession 'given by any company or express company, or by any person owning or controlling any such steamboat or vessel as is in the next paragraph mentioned, and where any privilege or concession is given by any such person or by any company or express company to any person or class of business, or in any part of Canada, the Board may order that such privilege or concession be discontinued, or modified, or granted to any other person or class of business, or in any other part of Canada, either the same or in a modified form.
" Steamboats to be subject to regulations of Board of Railway Commissioners.
" Tariffs, etc., to be submitted to Board."
" (A) 2. With respect to the traffic accommodation, classification of freight, traffic agreements, tolls, and tariffs to be furnished, made, entered into, and charged in connection with and by steamboats, and other vessels carrying passengers or freight, or both, from one port or place in Canada to another port or place in Canada, and with respect to any place where such steamboats and vessels shall call for traffic, the time of all and duration of stay and all tariffs, tolls, traffic agreements, and classifications of freight charged, entered into, or adopted in connection with any such steamboat or vessel shall be submitted to the Board."
I understand that you are now of the view that the ocean traffic overseas ought not to be mixed up with the same kind of regulation . which would apply from one port to another in Canada.
If the policy of water regulation be adopted at all, I would certainly think that you are right in this conclusion, and that the amendment you propose making to the draft above submitted, '1or to a port or place outside of Canada," be stricken out.

You ask my view as to whether or not the sections are sufficient. The question as jto whether there should be any regulation of water borne traffic, and whether the Board's powers should be extended in this direction, is one entirely of policy for Parliament and a matter on which I do not presume to advise or take any part; but if Parliament does adopt the principle, I would suggest that in addition to the amendment above set out, Section 358 be recast. The present Section 358, which is headed, " Water Traffic," would indicate thait the Board's activities in this connection are limited to the traffic on water of any railway company. As I understand it, your proposal is to regulate all water carriers, whether such carriers be or be not railway companies. To give effect to your intention, I would, as stated, recast this section, and provide as follows :-
"'Section 3'58. The provisions of this Act in respect of tolls, tariffs and joint tariffs shall, so far as deemed applicable by the Board, extend and apply to the traffic carried by any carrier (whether such carrier be or be not a railway company) by sea or by inland water, between any ports or places in Canada; and no freight or passenger rate shall be charged by any such water carrier in excess of the maximum rates from time to time approved by the Board; and no such water carrier shall engage in the business of transportation, whether of freight or of passengers, until such carrier shall have submitted to and the Board shall have approved its standard freight or passenger tariffs." Yours faithfully,
H. L. Drayton, Chief Commissioner. J. E. Armstrong, Esq., M.P.,
House of Commons, Ottawa.
That is the proposition which is now before the Committee. I may be asked my reasons for placing this matter under the control of the Bailway Commission. As every hon. gentleman knows, that commission is one of the best organized public bodies that we have in Canada. It has given most excellent service, and in spite of the fact that it was constituted some ten years ago, and that tens of thousands of questions of vital interest to the public have been brought before it from time to time, not one of the decisions it has rendered has been questioned on the floor of Parliament. This speaks well for the Bailway Commission, and therefore I cannot think of any more reliable body of men to have control of just such matters as we are considering to-night.
The reason for the creation of the Bailway Commission was this: It was found advisable to appoint a body altogether separate and apart from the Department of Bail-ways, that would stand between the public and the railways and deal out even-handed justice to the public in the face of the railway monopoly which then existed to a considerable extent. A somewhat similar situation exists to-day in regard to our water-

borne traffic. There is on our large inland lakes, and in connection with our coastwise trade, a monopoly which controls the traffic on those waters, and the eight millions of people scattered throughout this country are unable to organize and protect themselves from the combines that exist in connection with water transportation. It must be remembered that in my amendment I have eliminated the ocean-borne traffic, its provisions being confined to lake, river and coastwise trade. That object has been achieved by striking out the words " or to a port or place outside of Canada." If the amendment carries, and the Bill as amended goes back to the Senate and becomes law, then all the vessels operating on our inland ^waters and in connection with our coastwise trade will come under the control of the Railway Commission as regards the maximum rates which they charge.
In connection with ocean traffic, I hope, at an early date, to submit to Parliament a proposal, which should meet with the general approval of all the members, whereby a Board appointed by the Dominion Government, and a Board appointed by the Imperial Government, shall be able to control rates. In this regard I might call your attention to the fact that this Government, in 1912, appointed Sir Henry Drayton a commissioner to go overseas and investigate conditions in regard to the rates charged on ocean-borne traffic. Sir Henry Drayton made a thorough investigation and submitted a report to Parliament. In 1916 he prepared a still more exhaustive report in which he definitely and distinctly stated that it would be in the public interest to have a joint Board established in order that there might be a joint control between the Imperial and Dominion Governments of tolls and tariff agreements.
In 1912-13 the Imperial Government appointed a Royal Commission to investigate the natural resources, trade, and legislation of certain portions of His Majesty's Dominions. That commission travelled throughout the different Dominions beyond the seas, Canada amongst the rest, and, on its return to England, prepared a number of valuable reports. In 1917 it submitted its final report to the Imperial Parliament. I will just read one clause from page 128 to show the urgent need of taking action to control ocean-borne traffic:
Clause 538. Our investigations have satisfied us that in normal times the combination of shipowners is strong enough to limit the freedom of shippers, whose varied and detached interests make it difficult, if not impossible, for them to combine in any effective opposition,
186i
and that therefore, in principle, it is not desirable that the operations of the steamship companies should remain longer without some measure of Government supervision.
In this report you will find many recommendations, and it is with these recommendations that I intend to deal a little later on.
To-night we have before us the question of controlling the traffic on our inland waters and our coastwise trade, which is entirely separate from the matter to which I have been referring. It will be necessary for us to take into consideration the clauses 34 and 358 in connection with these amendments. They both deal with exactly the same subject, both being for the purpose of bringing our boats under the control of the Railway Commission. The Bill gives added powers to the Board of Railway Commissioners and we are most careful to see that in every detail we grant to the board complete control over traffic agreements and any concessions that may be made. We give them absolute control over almost everything connected with a railway system. Telegraphs, telephones, the wireless, and electrical development are all under Government control. But running alongside these great railway systems is another transportation system that has made wonderful progress within the last fifteen or twenty years. Last year there passed through the, Sault canals, American and Canadian, freights to the value of $85,000,000. As that traffic passes on down through lake Huron and the river St. Clair and into lake Erie, it increases in volume. Practically all the traffic is carried by boats that are absolutely free to charge whatever tolls and make whatever arrangements they please, and neither this nor any other Canadian Government can say a word. These boats can call or not at our ports, take goods or not, as they wish and are a law unto themselves. Let me call your attention to the increase in some of these rates. I will not have time to take many of them, but here, for instance, i,s a list of lake rates on wheat from Fort William and Port Arthur to Montreal for the undermentioned seasons of navigation:

All right; it will be for the hon. gentleman to show that the statement I have given is not correct. In 1909 the steamboats on our inland waters were able to carry that same kind of grain from Port Arthur to Montreal for two cents a bushel, and it has been stated that they carried it for less than that. In face of the fact that these increases have been going on from year to year there seems to be no limit to them, and there is no reason in the world why they should not charge 15 or 20 cents a bushel. They could possibly reach that limit and I have no doubt that they would be only too glad to have that rate.
I shall show a little later on the enormous profits that some of these companies are making. It would appear they are taking full advantage of the opportunity confronting them. I repeat again, that these organizations are under no control whatsoever, and all that I am asking in this amendment is that the Railway Commission shall have the power to declare what the maximum rates shall be.
In the United States they have complete control over their boats engaged in inland water and coastwise trade. Not only have they that control, but I have under my hand a complete set of the ocean rates from the United States ports. Let me call your attention to their legislation. Under a statute of the most drastic character they absolutely control their boats engaged on inland waters and coastwise trade. For
fMr. J. E. Armstrong,]
instance under this statute on April 18, 1919, the Shipping Board at Washington issued the following statement:
Rates for shipment on the Great Lakes this season for ore, grain and coal were formally approved by the Shipping- Board to-day as follows:-Ore 80 cents a ton; coal, 42J cents a ton; grain from Lake Superior to Lake Brie and from Lake Michigan to Lake Erie, April and May loading, 3J cents and 3 cents per bushel respectively; September, October and November grain loading, 3} cents and 3 cents respectively; and December grain loading, including winter storage of vessels, 5 cents and 5 cents respectively; grain rates to Georgian Bay and Goderich were fixed at one-half cent per bushel; to Port Huron one-half cent per bushel and to Collingwood one-half cent per bushel under the Lake Brie rate. The rate to Detroit was made the same as to Lake Erie ports.
In Canada we have no such condition -of agairs. Our shipowners can continue charging their ten cents or twelve cents a bushel or more if they please, and we are powerless to control them. Just a few words in regard to this Shipping Act which was passed by Congress in 1916. It is chapter 451 of the United States statutes and is intituled " An Act to establish a United States. Shipping Board for the purpose of encouraging, developing and creating a naval auxiliary and a naval reserve and a merchant marine to meet the requirements of the commerce of the United States with its territories and possessions, and with foreign countries; to regulate carriers by water in the foreign and interstate commerce of the United States; and for other purposes. This statute deals with the transfer of government-owned vessels to the board and the operation of American merchant vessels; it defines what is a common carrier; specifies the penalty for violation of the provisions of the Act-the authority of the board to approve or disapprove of rates-common carriers not to lower rates by unfair means -tariffs to be filed and displayed-through rates-restrictions on increasing charges- and so on. I might go on reading page after page of this Aot, but I have indicated sufficient to show that it is of the most drastic nature and that it covers absolutely all boats owned, operated and controlled in the United States. A number of amendments have been made to that Act since 1916, every one of them in the direction of giving still greater control over their water-borne traffic. But we have made no effort whatever to control our water-borne traffic. It is said that the Railway Commission is given control over the through rates of boats owned controlled and operated by the railways of Canada. That is

true, but they have only control over the through rate, and if that rate is charged without any unjust or unfair discrimination there is no cause for action on the part of the commission. As far as the railways are concerned, they have not appeared before any of the committees in opposition to this measure, and as far as 1 can learn they do not oppose it in any way.
But why should we allow the Railway Commission to have control over a certain portion of our water-borne traffic and not place the whole of it under their control ? We have 8,500 vessels under Dominion register, employing 45,000 men. In this Act that we are to pass to-night, the railway men who are assisting in the operations of the railroads in Canada are surrounded with all sorts of safeguards. During the hearings before the Select Committee, those men sat day after day, week after week, and month after month, listening to the arguments to see that their rights were protected; while, on the contrary, the 45,000 employees,, a,s far as I can learn, are absolutely at the mercy of the vessel owners. We assist water transportation in every way; we surround these men with special laws for their benefit. Not only do we do that, but within the last month when a member called attention to the fact that the United States had forbidden Canadian vessels to do any coastwise trade on their coast, the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce said that owing to that fact similar restrictions would be placed upon boats owned in the United States coming to do a coastwise trade on our coasts. So that these men are surrounded by every conceivable protection and are in the position of an absolute monopoly.
We protect our marine interests from foreign shippers; we buoy and light our rivers; we dredge them and we deepen our harbours; we build docks, piers, breakwaters, canals,' without end, until we have expended over $400,000,000 of the people's money on these great enterprises. And in the face of that we find members on both sides of the House asking the Minister of Public Works to continue the expenditure of enormous sums of money on such works in different parts of the Dominion. What for? In order to aid navigation. But are we to continue this expenditure? The more money we expend the higher go the rates, and we are in the unfortunate position that we have no control over these vessel owners as to what they may charge or the manner in which they conduct their affairs. The people Of Canada do not receive any interest on this money. We have abolished
the tolls on our canals. We are spending a million and a half a year in order to operate these public works, all aids to navigation, but there is no apparent return to the people; the rates have been constantly increased rather than reduced. In addition to this, we have built elevators at Port Arthur, Fort William, Montreal and St. John. We have spent immense sums to facilitate the loading and unloading ot grain. The capacity of the vessels has increased enormously. Not so many years ago we thought that a vessel which would carry 100,000 bushels of grain had reached about the limit of carrying capacity, but vessels are to-day carrying down our lakes 500,000 bushels in each cargo. When the Welland canal is opened these boats will be in a much more favourable position than they are in to-day. It is generally understood that rates on water-borne traffic should be at least one-third the rates by rail, but we find that the rates for waterborne traffic are kept as close as possible to the rail rates, those interested in the operation of these vessels desiring to make every dollar they can out of the people. We have expended enormous sums of money uj)on the construction of elevators in our western provinces. We have provided a grain commission. We see that the rates charged in these elevators are fair and reasonable and that the rates on the railways which carry the grain from the elevators to Port Arthur and Fort William are the very lowest that can be charged. From the day the grain is turned over to the vessel men at Port Arthur and Fort William and is loaded into their vessels until it reaches its destination -our own markets or the markets of the world-not one word can any one say with regard to the transportation charges made on that grain. That is surely not a reasonable or a fair position for the people of the West to be placed in. As I shall show you, the people of the East are in the same humiliating position. Why control only part of our transportation system? These undertakings have called for vast expenditures of money. No individual or corporate enterprise would undertake them. Canada has undertaken them; what return has she? An unregulated, irresponsible mercantile marine. Unless you place on the statute-book some such legislation as I am urging, you will continue to be subjected to excessive charges.
Either regulate and control this organization, or open the door to competitors. Expenses of carriage by water are small as compared with the expenses of carriage by rail. The shipowners have no roadbeds or tun-

nels or bridges to keep in repair, no terminal stations to maintain, no telegraphs or telephones to operate. Before the Committee these men told us of the severe storms that occur on our lakes and on our coasts, and how they materially interfere with the operation of the vessels. But have they taken into consideration the fact that during the winter season the railroads are able to do only about sixty per cent of the business they are capable of doing during the summer months? The amount of money invested in boats compared with that invested in railways is very small. Take, for instance, the 2,200 miles of splendid waterway that reaches on up into the heart of this continent. The first 1,000 miles from the Gulf of St. Lawrence to Montreal may be traversed with perfect safety by vessels drawing thirty feet of water, and vessels drawing fourteen feet of water can proceed 1,200 miles further to Port Arthur and Fort William. When the Welland canal is completed a much better condition will be brought about. The investment in Canadian steamships plying on this route would, at a fair estimate, not exceed $50,000,000, while the cost of a railway covering about the same distance, at $100,000 a mile-which was the cost of the railway most recently built by the Dominion-would exceed $200,000,000. I make this comparison merely to show that while these men are carrying on their business as I have indicated, the expense connected with the operation of their vessels is small compared with the cost of our railways.

I have here a great deal of correspondence with regard to this matter, hut I shall only glance over some of it hurriedly to direct attention to what is going on in different parts of this country. On April 20 of this * Lib. j_ Armstrong.!
