I have here another letter from the President of the Niagara District Board of Trade. Then there is the following telegram from Petrolia:

Between what points is the 7i cent rate?
Mr. J! E. ARMSTRONG: From Port Arthur to Montreal, I understand.

The hon. gentleman stated that the vessel would carry 300,000 bushels from Port Arthur to Montreal, and the rate as stated by Mr. Horne was 71 cents. What I wish to say is this, that there is no vessel that can go from Port Arthur to Montreal carrying 300,000 bushels.

This gentleman was a steamboat owner and the minister must surely know him. If he does not the representatives from Port Arthur and Fort William can vouch for his standing in Port Arthur. He says: " The lower lake ports." He might mean Port Colborne, but the rate is 71 cents. A few minutes ago I showed that the United States had absolute control over their vessels and that their grain is carried from Port Arthur and Fort William down to Buffalo, a greater distance than to Port Colborne, for 31 cents. The people of Canada must feel humiliated at being compelled to pay such extortionate rates in the face of prevailing conditions.
I do not want to take up much of the time of the Committee in reading these letters, but they are all urging that these clauses be passed. I have here a communication from Mr. J. T. Small, barrister, of Toronto, strongly urging that these boats be placed under the control of the Railway Commission. This is a letter from a prominent citizen in the town of Sarnia:-
From our experience this year as shippers with the Northern Navigation Company, it is more imperatively necessary than it ever has been before, that this legislation should pass. As matters' stand now, shippers have no rights that the steamship lines in particular pay any attention to. Rates have gone up to the limit. Service, while fairly satisfactory is nothing as good as it should b;. "What does this, mean to your home county?
George French.

This is a communication to the Department of the Secretary of State from the Government of British Columbia:
Certified copy of a report of a committee of the Honourable the Executive Council, approved by His Honour the Lieutenant Governor on the 26th day of March, 1919.
The committee of Council submit for the approval of His Honour the Lieutenant Governor a resolution of the Legislative Assembly yof the province of British Columbia, of the 24th instant, as follows :-
That, In the opinion of this House it is desirable that the rates of lake and river transportation systems owned and controlled by the Canadian Pacific Railway in British Columbia should be under the control of the Railway Commission of Canada.
Be it further resolved, that an humble address he presented to His Honour the Lieutenant Governor, praying that a copy of the foregoing resolution foe forwarded to the Honourable the Secretary of State for Canada.
The Committee advise that a copy of this minute be forwarded to the Honourable the Secretary of State of Canada.
J. H. MaoLean,
Clerk, Executive Council.
I might go on reading these communications, but I do not care to take up the time of the committee. It is true that Canada's waterways have been the chief factor in building up towns and cities along them. These are the channels through which pass much of our raw materials and manufactured products. We must, therefore, control these great national transportation facilities, and we must not turn over this splendid heritage of the many to be exploited for the benefit of the few. We must consider the interest of the producer at one end and the consumer at the other. Reduced rates will mean cheaper food for our people with commercial development all along our waterways. With boats under control, fair profits to boat owners will be given, and the producer and consumer will be greatly benefited. Vessel men are constantly asking for improvements. (Our past expenditures would have been justified had rates been reduced, but the opposite has been 'the case. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvel!), it is true, voted against this amendment in Committee, but inside of a few hours he was in the House voting away money for the improvements of these great waterways and for the benefit of the vessel men. There has been circulated among the members of the House of Commons and the Senate a pamphlet carefully prepared by one of the solicitors of the Canada Steamship Company.

By whom?
Mr.. J. E. ARMSTRONG: Mr. King.
He is not the solicitor.
He is solicitor for the Dominion Marine Association. Is not that correct?
Yes.

He represents at least ninety per cent of the vessels on our inland waters, and my hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol) knows it. This pamphlet was not very complimentary to me. It held up to ridicule my efforts in the pa-st in connection with this measure. It is true that at different times during the last six years I have brought forward this measure. It is also true that the Railway Act which is now under consideration has not yet been passed. But I do not see why I should be condemned for the action I have taken in the matter. I should like to give a brief account of what has taken place.
In the year 1912-13 members on both sides of the House called attention to the enormous increase in freight rates on our inland waters and on our ocean-borne commerce. Considerable time of the House was taken up in debating the question, and a Special Committee was formed which had under consideration the consolidation of the Railway Act. While it was under consideration, the Saskatchewan Government appointed a commission to investigate freight rates on our inland waters and ocean-borne commerce. That investigation took place, and I was able to submit to the Railway Committee in 1914, a statement in regard to the work of that oominis-sion. I also laid before the Committee a letter from Mir. R. McKenzie, secretary of the Manitoba Crain Growers' Association, reading as follows:
I am in receipt of your favour of the 20th inst., urging me to appear before a Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons who have the consolidation of the Railway Act under consideration. I did not receive the' telegram from you which you state you sent under the same date as letter.
I would foe very .pleased of an, opportunity to appear on behalf of the *Manitoba Grain Growers' Association before the Committee on the important question of the consolidation of the Railway Act, more especially clause 358 of the Bill to which you drew my attention. It appears to me that the Railway Commission or any other foody have not effective control on export rates unless that same body can also control the rates on vessels that are a pant of a through transportation system. It is a simple matter of bookkeeping for the railways to apportion a loss made on the railway, and make up on the water portion of the through system.

I also placed before the Committee the following statement from a manufacturer in the city of Sarnia:
As you are possibly aware, there is a most unjust dkcrimm tion against manufacturers situated as we are. At the present time, steamship companies will carry freight from Montreal to the head of the Lakes, we are told, at the same rates as we pay from Sarnia to the head of the Lakes. We know for a fact that there is an existing rate of 10J cents from Cleveland to Fort Wil iam, while we pay 16^ cents from Sarnia. This is one ease showing the unjust dis:rimination made under the present me the d. Where this affects a manufacture:-, such as ourselves, it would avail the manufacturers of the Fame commodities as we make, down in Montreal or Hamilton, to enter into a competition of territory, which, by our natural location, should be ours.
On the other hand, for all freight going east by train, we have to pay a much higher rate over these lines, and we cannot compete with the manufacturer, such as a fence company, in Montreal or Hamilton in its own district, while they themselves can ship their commodity into our territory at the same rates as we ourselves.
I submitted also a communication from the Western Co-operative Fruit Company, resolutions passed by a company of fruit growers in Western Ontario, and a letter to Mr. K. F. Green, M.P., from the British Columbia Fruit Growers' Association, all strongly supporting the measure.
I should like to quote the finding of the commission appointed by the Saskatchewan Government:
This Commission reports that the grain ol Canada pays more freight to r a:h Liverpool than does the grain of any other country in the world ; also that there has been practically no change since 1909 in the cost of transpc ing a carload' of wheat to Fort William or Port Arthur and selling it on commission. . .
	Were Winnipeg to Fort William the
ultimate market for our wheat, it would he unnecessary to pursue the inquiry east of these points. Some of our wheat is finally disposed of at Winnipeg, of course, but the great hulk of it is not. Moreover, the price received for that which goes the farthest is what sets the price for the remainder throughout the season of heaviest marketing. It therefore concerns the farmer even more than it concerns anyone else what the relation is between the Winnipeg market and the importing markets of Europe, for upon the transportation and oth r connecting links between these markets will the price received by the farmer in one part depend.
Those were some of the statements placed before the Committee in 1914. In 1915-16 the war was on, and as this measure was looked upon as contentious, it was not taken up. In 1917, although the war was still on, the Railway Act was taken up by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Cochrane) and passed this House, but was held up in the Senate. During the discussion that took place I was able to submit
many important matters to the Committee, among which was a letter I received from Mr. P. P. Woodbridge, secretary of the United Farmers of Alberta, as follows:
I am in receipt of yours of the 20th instant, together with the copy of Bill No. 2 and notes on same.
After discussing the proposed amendments with our president and several other members of our executive who happened to be available,
I beg to advise you that we are entirely in sympathy with -the object of clause 358 and unanimously endorse same. We believe, however, that as at present worded, the clause opens the way for a legal action as to the extent of its meaning.
Lines 2 and 3, clause 3'58, read at present,
" extend and apply to traffic carried by any railway company," etc. We believe that to make this clause really effective it must be made to cover all water traffic, whether carried in boats owned by railway o>r other company or individual, and would respectifuHy suggest that the word ' railway * be eliminated from this clause, making it read, ' traffic carried by any company or individual,' etc., etc., or whatever amendment your committee might suggest which would affect the purpose hereinbefore outlined.
T merely call attention to this for the purpose of showing that I did make an earnest effort to bring this matter before Parliament from time to time. Then again at the present session instead of proceeding with the Bill Which I introduced at an early period, I thought it was not wise to take up time with the various stages that would be necessary, and therefore, for the purpose of securing prompt action, I placed my amendment before the special committee of the House. It was defeated by a small majority, and to-night I believe I am acting in the public interest in bringing forward that amendment in Committee of the Whole and having a vote upon the question.
During the war every other country took measures to control its shipping but we apparently made no effort in that direction. The farmers, manufacturers, and shippers of Canada have been compelled to pay fifty, one hundred and fifty, and two hundred per cent more for the carriage of their goods by water than they formerly were compelled to pay. We are giving credits to Belgium, Italy, Greece, and Eumania. to the extent of tens of millions of dollars for the purpose . of carrying the products of farm and factory to those markets. But when you take into consideration the enormous tolls that are exacted on the inland vessels, and on the ocean-borne commerce, it is utterly impossible for us to expect, unless this amendment is accepted, that Canadian manufacturers and shippers will receive the benefit which they should receive

from the existing facilities. If this amendment is voted down it means keeping open the door for a further exploitation of the country's resources.
Let me call attention to some of the profits that these steamship owners have been making during the last few years. In 1912 the Canada Steamship Company formed a merger of six groups of vessels, the estimated value of which at that time was some $6,000,000. The company was floated for $12,500,000 of preferred stock, $12,000,000 of common stock, and $6,000,000 of'bonds. And what happened? The rates increased. In 1914, I asked one of the prominent vessel owners what the increase in rate? amounted to in 1913, and he said about twenty per cent. The rates have kept on increasing year after year until these men claim today that they have a capital investment of-or at least that the value of their industry is-$38,000,000, and they are paying the interest on $30,000,000 of that money. They are paying the interest not only on the preferred stock and on the bonds, but on the common stock as well. Let me give you a statement by Mr. Carruthers, president *of the company, but who resigned during the present year, as it appears in the Cana-[DOT]dian Railway and Marine World of last *March. Mr. Carruthers left Montreal for the Pacific coast some time prior to the *proposed meeting, and before doing so made the following remarks:
I cannot admit the propriety of paying such a dividend, for several reasons, and in this attitude have received Mr. Newman's consistent sympathy and support. My principal reason for adopting the attitude described was that I considered the company's best interests were bound up in maintaining the dividend position of its premier capital issue, the preferred stock. In other words, this issue should be strengthened during a period of exceptional earnings, with such a reserve backing that the continuance of the regular rate would be assured for some years to come. My contention is that the disbursement should not be made until there is a strong liquid reserve behind the preferred. It was not the idea of the organizers of the company at its inception that the common should receive anything in the way of dividend until the company had gone through a period of years of experience, which would prove its earning capacity beyond question. In order that my attitude should not prove an embarrassment to the board, and so that the decision to declare the dividend might be considered unanimous, I have decided to resign the presidency^ and also from the board, and Mr. Newman joins me in my retirement.
That is a pretty strong statement made *by the president in regard to the Canada *Steamship Company. But when the company are not only paying dividends on all *this stock, but have a surplus of $5,000,000, 
*and claim that their assets amount to *$38,000,000, hon. gentlemen can readily see *whether they have been doing a reasonable *or a fair business within the last six years. I know for a fact that many members of *this House have been receiving telegrams *and letters urging them to oppose this *amendment, and it must be expected that *practically every port in this country has *supporters of this steamship organization. *You can depend upon it that they are not *going to be content with the sending of a *few telegrams or letters voicing their opposition,.
* Now what else do I find in the report of this company? The capital stock I have *already stated, and the depreciation reserve *is $3,506,000. They paid in business profits *war tax $960,000, and a surplus was left of *$5,009,000. These figures show what one *company can accomplish within a period of six short years. Is it to be imagined that *a company that cleans up $30,000,000 in five or six years wants this legislation adopted? *Remember that Canada is going to do a *greater business on water than ever before. I expect a great expansion of our foreign trade when we control our trade routes, and our manufacturers and our shipping will develop. Off this legislation passes it will help the man who tills the soil, and it will help the man who runs a factory or carries a dinner pail. If it should be defeated the responsibility must rest on the heads of those who vote against it. It is a safe, sane and business like proposition. It will provide control of our waterways in addition to the control of our railways. The shippers scattered throughout Canada cannot organize into a monopoly. We must therefore trust to the Railway Commission to look after their interests. I therefore appeal to every member of this committee to vote for this amendment. By doing so they will protect the interest of the many against the avarieiousness and selfishness of the few.
In the early stages of my remarks I drew attencion to the fact that the amendment which I propose does not ask for the control of ocean freight rates; it is confined entirely to lake, river, canal and coastwise trade. Therefore, when hon. gentlemen are casting votes for this amendment they must remember they are voting for the control by the Railway Commission of maximum freight rates. By that I mean that the vessel owners will be able to give as low a rate as they choose below the maximum, but that tlhe Railway Commission will have the power to establish maximum freight

rates. Surely this is not an unreasonable request to make of this committee. I therefore strongly urge the members of this committee to vote for my amendment in order that we may control the great steamship monopolies that now exist in our country.
I beg to move to amend clause 34 by adding after subparagraph (a) in the fourth line of the said clause the following subparagraphs :
(A) 1. With respect to any privilege or concession given by any company or express company or by any person owning or controlling any such steamboat or vessel as is in the next paragraph mentioned, and where any privilege or concession is given by any such person or by any company or express company to any person or class of business or in any part of Canada, the Board may order that such privilege or concession be discontinued or modified or granted to any other person or class of business, or in any other part of Canada, either the same or in a modified form.
(A) 2. With respect to the traffic accommodation, classification of freight, traffic agreements, tolls and tariffs to be furnished, made, entered into and charged in connection with and by steamboats, and other vessels carrying passengers or freight or both from one port or place in Canada to another port or place in Canada and with respect to any place where such steamboats and vessels shall call for traffic, the time of call and duration of stay and all tariffs, tolls, traffic agreements and classifications of freight, charged, entered into or adopted in connection with any such steamboat or vessel shall he submitted to the Board.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. EEID (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not detain the House at any great length in reply to the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) on this question. The Railway Bill is a very important one and one that has been before the House for the last two sessions. For a year or so previous to that we had men employed on this Act in order that it might be put in proper form. It is important that it should pass the House during the present session. It is urgent for many reasons. It is urgent on account of the necessity for the protection of the employees in connection with the operation of railways. It is also urgent in connection with the operation of the railways as a whole, and in the interest of the traffic that is carried. For these reasons, I hope that the Bill may go through during the present session. It has passed this House with the exception of the clause that the hon. member has referred to, and clause 374, which has been left over on account of the interest in it of the city of Toronto, the Hydro-Electric Commission and the Toronto and Niagara Power Company.
It is a very important question, that the hon. member has brought before the Committee. I am sorry that, his Bill, to which he has referred, was not proceeded with during the session, for the reason that we could have given more time to the discussion of the question and probably could have brought forth more facts bearing upon it than we are able to elicit this evening. The hon. member has referred to the letter of Sir Henry Drayton. From the tone of his remarks you would come to the conclusion that he is under the impression that Sir Henry Drayton is in favour of this amendment being passed by this House.

I read the lettei
and the letter distinctly says that he does not assume any responsibility.

I admit that he does not assume any responsibility. But there is a part of the letter from which the hon. gentleman read that I think is very important in connection with this matter. On page 2 Sir Henry Drayton says:
If the policy of water regulation he adopted at all-
That gives me the impression that Sir Henry Drayton is not altogether in favour of the amendment as proposed by the hon. member.
He does not take a position one way or the other.

That part of the letter emphasizes very strongly that he is not altogether in favour of the amendment. The hon. member leads the House to believe that the traffic by water between Port Arthur and Montreal is not now, and never has been, under the Railway Commission, and that the water traffic rates on wheat and other products have never been under any regulation.
As far as steamboats are concerned.

As far as steamboats are concerned. In the Railway Act, which has been in force for many years, we have a clause:
The provisions of this Act in respect of tolls, tariffs and joint tariffs shall, so far as they are applicable, extend to the traffic carried by any company by sea or iby inland water, between any ports or places in Canada, if the company owns, charters, uses, maintains or works, or is a party to any arrangement for using, maintaining or working vessels for carrying traffic by sea or by inland water 'between any such ports or places.
It is a well known fact that the Canadian Northern Railway Company until two or three years ago, when their vessels were

taken, or disposed of, for purposes in connection with the war, had a fleet of steamers plying between Port Arthur and Montreal carrying grain, and therefore they came under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners. If there were any complaints about the freight rates between Port Arthur and Montreal, they have been for many years past, and are now, under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners in so far as this provision applies to vessels owned or controlled by railway companies.
Why object to this clause, then?

I am coming to that a little later. One of the strongest points that the hon. member has urged why this amendment should pass is that it may afford reduced rates on the wheat shipments that come from the West to the East and for transportation overseas. The Canadian Pacific, the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Northern for years not only had their own vessels, but had the chartering of other vessels. That traffic has been as much under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners as any part of the traffic going to Montreal. I only wish to mention that fact to assure hon. members from the West that, there is nothing in the argument that freight rates between Port Arthur and Montreal may be lowered or changed from what they have been in the past.
Let me also take up at this point the hon. member's statement in reference to freight rates. He quoted the rates between the years 1911 and 1918. In 1911 the lowest average was between 4.24 and 6.50 between Port Arthur and Montreal. In 1912, if I took his statement down correctly, the average rate was about 5.77, or practically the same as in 1911. In the years 1913, 1914 and 1915 the rates were practically the same. In 1916 they commenced to jump; in 1917 they again increased, and in 1918 they still farther advanced. That is one of the reasons why the hon. member argues that these vessels should be put under the Board of Railway Commissioners. If it had only been on inland waters that these rates had been increased the argument might hold good, but the rates have increased not only between Port Arthur and Montreal but between Atlantic ports and British ports where the increases were far more in proportion than they were inland.
Three times as much.

The hon. member has asked me a question which I am quite satisfied he must know I could not answer offhand. Had he given me notice I would be prepared to answer it. I do not know whether the question has ever been brought before the Railway Commission as to the regulation of a water rate between Port Arthur and Montreal. But they have power to regulate the railway freight rates, and they have also power to regulate the rates on freight originating on a Canadian railway and carried through to destination on a vessel owned or chartered by the railway company. Supposing the Railway Commission were to fix a certain rate for vessels plying between Port Arthur and Montreal to apply to all Canadian-owned vessels, our neighbours to the south of us could take advantage of it and secure the traffic, and it would be impossible for us to interfere. Let me give you an instance. Today when a vessel goes into Port Arthur she does not know what rate she is going to get. We will say that the rate is fixed by the Board of Railway Commissioners at 5 cents from Port Arthur to Montreal. The Canadian vessel cannot take any less than that rate.
Is it not the maximum rate that we are asking to have fixed?

All right. At all events whatever rate is fixed, she applies for that
rate. Look at the competition our vessels have to-day at Montreal. If an American vessel goes into Port Arthur-that is, assuming she can go through the canals- and she finds that she can get a higher rate by taking that grain to Montreal than by taking it to Buffalo, I will tell you what her owners will do, because I know what has been done in the past, and I have no doubt it will be done in the future.
They take .a rate of three cents a bushel from Port Arthur to Ogdensburg, New York. The grain is there placed in an elevator and subsequently sent on barges to Montreal-and the American company can quote a. rate which is a shade less than the rate quoted by the Canadian vessels. In other words, American vessels may carry that grain in American, bottoms from one Canadian port to another Canadian port, and they cannot be interfered with. That is [DOT]the competition that the Canadian bottoms have to meet to-day and will have to meet in the future. If there is any question about fixing the rates charged on Canadian vessels from Port Arthur to Buffalo, the American vessel men will simply say to the shippers in the West: ship your grain to Duluth and we will take it from Duluth [DOT]to Buffalo.
We have very many people who are interested in water-borne traffic. Individuals or companies have put their money into vessels which ply on our inland waters. These enterprises are not public utilities, [DOT]and to place them undeT the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission would, in my opinion, interfere with shipbuilding in the future. The jurisdiction which is exercised by the Railway Commission so far as through traffic is concerned would seem to cover any possible chance of the imposition of extraordinary freight rates. I have watched the steamboat business .in the past with a great deal of interest. Until the war started, I venture to say, the profits of vessel men were not very high; none of them made extraordinary profits. I hardly think it is fair to take the last three or four years of the war in order to show that excess profits have been made.
The hon. member read a great many letters expressing the opinion that his amendment should be adopted and that we should bring these vessels under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission. It would take me an hour to read all the communications I have received from individuals and Boards of Trade protesting against any such legislation. If the amend-

meat was adopted, it would interfere in a great many ways with our other inland water transportation. Privately-owned tramp vessels running from Montreal to Port Arthur are glad to get freight for inland ports at very low rates; in fact, they take it at any rates	they can possibly
get. They take freight also at low rates to Port Arthur, because in doing so they are just that much ahead. Again, if this amendment is adopted it will affect the operation of motorboats which carry passengers on our inland lakes, and other waters. On the St. Lawrence river, among the Thousand Islands and all the way between Montreal and Kingston, motor-boats carry passengers during the summer months. Under my hon. friend's proposal these boats could not carry passengers without first submitting their standard rates to the Board of Railway Commissioners.
I do not think the adoption of this amendment would be of any advantage to the shippers of the West. If I thought for a moment that such rates were being charged between Port Arthur and Montreal as were prejudicial to the people of the West I would be the first to introduce an amendment, or to bring down legislation to correct the wrong. But I am satisfied that the effect of the amendment would not be to reduce the rates. The Canadian Government owns 13,000 miles of railway-if it takes over the Grand Trunk it will own 20,000 miles. These railways operate steamboats, and the whole system is owned by the Government and controlled by Parliament. The freight rates between Port Arthur and the Georgian bay ports are subject to control; the rates between Port Arthur and Montreal can be controlled by the railways. As it has not been shown that there has been any unfairness, I think it would not be in the interest either of the public or of the mercantile marine of this country to have the Bill changed as proposed in the amendment.

Coming from a
city situated on one of the Great Lakes, I desire to say something on this question. I unfortunately was not present while the arguments were being put forth in the committee from time to time, as business called me away. The only arguments 1 have heard in favour of vessels being placed under the jurisdiction of the Railway Board are what I have heard here tonight, and no arguments from those who ship or receive goods by water have been produced to-night. Therefore, if persons who ship or receive goods by water are satisfied, I do not see why other persons should complain, and they utterly fail to produce evidence that anybody has suffered on account of the rates. The hon. member for East Lambton seems to be endeavouring to show that rail and water transportation are in the same position. They are in different positions entirely. Railways are established in certain districts and have monopolies of those districts, and if they were not under the jurisdiction of the Railway Board they could charge whatever rates they saw fit, and the Railway Board was appointed for the purpose of controlling those rates. As regards water transportation, the water is there; I can use it; you can use it; anybody who likes can use it. People can charge rates in competition with each other, and if any one is charging a higher rate than is commonly charged, competition will regulate the matter. I have not found any argument produced by the hon. member except in a circular letter that he sent out., and the argument produced there is as hopelessly weak as the argument he has made here to-night to convince any hon. member to vote in support of the amendment. The first paragraph in that circular letter goes on to show that all boats owned by the railway companies are under the Railway Board. It goes on to point out that shippers may take goods or leave them or refuse to call at certain points, or in other words, just do as they like. The hon. member has not undertaken to show that the boats referred to have ever refused to accept goods or have ever taken goods and charged an unreasonable price, but he makes a statement so broad that it would be utterly
impossible to corner him so as to show that there was nothing in his argument. The next paragraph goes on to show that our coastal regulations give our vessels every advantage over foreign vessels and that as far as possible the right has been retained for the use of our vessels. This might have a tendency to increase rates instead of diminishing them, but such has not been the case. The water rates have, I consider, been very low, and I can assure the Committee that there is not in the city of Hamilton, from which I come, a firm which would not vote against the amendment. The next paragraph goes on to cite that the Government has established elevators in the West and has appointed a grain commissioner to grade the farmer's product; that they control the freight rates to Fort William, and when the grain reaches Fort William they are obliged to turn it over to a group of vessel owners who are not under any Government control whatever. The facts in connection with the case are different from what the hon. member has been endeavouring to lead the Committee to believe. The rates charged by the Canadian Pacific on wheat from Regina to Fort William is 15 cents per bushel; that is a distance of 777 miles, and when they turn this grain over to the group of vessel owners referred to, the latter carry the wheat from Fort William to Montreal, about twice the distance, for half the rate charged by the Canadian Pacific from Regina to Fort William. That practically means that the rate on the lakes is 25 per cent of what it is on the railways under the Railway Board. If that be true, and I will challenge the hon. member to contradict it, surely the hon. member does not want a vessel to carry freight for less than'25 per cent of the rate charged by the railways. If he does, he is expecting too much.
There is another clause in this circular sent out by the hon. member in which he says that he thinks the freight rates should be one-third less by water than by rail. I should like to read the last part of Mr Payne's letter on that point:
Speaking broadly, it might be assumed with some degree of soundness that freight rates on our inland waterways are about one-third of that of the railways.
I will now read a letter from the Hamilton branch of the Canadian Manufacturers Association dated May 9, 1919, with reference to the Armstrong amendment:
This matter has been very seriously tik^n up with the Transportation Dept, of the Harnil-

opinion of these men who know the situation thoroughly from a shipping standpoint should be respected. They have given this matter careful thought and consideration, and they find that it is absolutely impossible for the city and district of Quebec to continue in the path of progress upon which they have started if such -an enactment as the one under consideration is passed. I ask the Committee to very carefully view the matter, not only from the local but from the national standpoint, and consider whether or not it is a good thing to stifle the progress and the industry of one of our national ports.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
On behalf of the city of Port Arthur I ask the Committee to reject this amendment. The people of that city have taken a very active interest in (this proposal both last year and this year. They have studied the question carefully from the standpoint of the vital effect it will have upon their interests. Pott Arthur is dependent upon transportation from ship to railway, and the merchants, shippers, -wholesalers, and other interests of that city, after careful consideration, are unalterably opposed to this legislation and to any interference with the vessel trade. One dislikes to differ with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Armstrong) in presenting anything to this House because of his particularly genial manner in so doing, but I think -he has not the experience in this matter of those who have always been dealing in ships and in the trade connected therewith. I do not intend reflecting in- any way upon- the Railway Board; but one cannot help thinking that if the railways are brought -into competition with public bodies before the Board on the question as to what rates are t-o prevail, the influence of the railroads in their endeavour to -raise the rates, must necessarily affect the board. A vessel to-day will carry a cargo equal to five train loads. Necessarily the freight rate by rail between the same points must always be much higher for that reason, and it will be to the interest of the railroads to pull up the freight rate by water, and especially in the case of through rates, instead of, by virtue of the competition, pulling it down.
The point made by the hon. member tor Hamilton ('Mr. -Stewart) that you cannot in the case of these vessels have fixed rates is very true. There are times on the lakes when vessels are operating that it becomes either a question of taking freight at a very low rate or taking water ballast. For years

before the war during the summer time we had coal coming from Cleveland to Port Arthur at thirty cents a ton, simply because the vessel owners would rather carry coal at that rate than carry water ballast. How can you have -fixed rates unless those rates are regulated each month of the year? -and then you could not fix the rates definitely for each month according to the business that was offered. Many o-f the wholesalers and dealers in the West bring their goods to Port Arthur and store them there-I have seen acres- of barbed wire so stored

waiting to be handled west in the winter, thus taking advantage of the low summer freight rate by boat. I am perfectly satisfied that if -the Railway Commission is given the power to control the rates on these vessels the result will simply be to destroy competition, to interfere with the freedom that ought to prevail, and will tend to raise the rates. If there is anything the railroads desire it is to get control of the docks and get control, if they can, of the boats, and as long as you have a man who is able to build a boat and who is willing to enter the business and get what freight he can, and can get deliverance at a dock, you need not fear any monopoly as you do in the case of the railroads. I hope the Committee will consider very carefully before it passes any of the amendments suggested.
M-r. CA-S-GRAIN: I would like to say a few words in reference to what the Hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. J. D. Reid) and the hon. member for Quebec (Mr. Power) have said. Coming from the district of Quebec where there is a large amount of traffic being carried by small boats plying between Quebec and lower St. Lawrence ports, I have followed this discussion with a good deal of interest. At nearly every place in my county along the banks of the St. Lawrence, there are five or six of these small boats plying between Quebec and these different places. These vessels have always made such freight and passenger rates as to them seemed fit and proper according to the circumstances and in accordance with the law of supply and demand. If this amendment were put into force these people would be placed in competition with large steamboat companies and also with the railway companies which would iiave the immediate effect of putting nearly every one of the small vessel owners out of business. It has always been deemed wise to leave water transportation free. As far as I am aware there have never been any excessive rates charged and I do not see why this amendment should

be adopted. It is not very often that I vote for the Government, but on the present occasion I find myself under the neces- " sity of voting with the Minister of Railways.

I have noticed that the amendment has commanded a good deal of attention throughout Canada and that since its first introduction it has been followed by no class of people more closely than by the shippers on our lakes and rivers. It has been suggested to-night that almost every person Who has made representations to this committee or to the House has been opposed to the amendment as brought down. I would remind the committee that the amendments that the hon. member has submitted in the past are different from the amendment which we have before us to-night and that all the arguments which have been made against the amendment seem to be based on the fact that the hon. gentleman fixed a minimum charge in connection with transporting persons and goods over these routes. It was also argued in the special railway committee the other day that should this Government assume the responsibility, through the Railway Board, of establishing rates on the lakes it might interfere with the shipment of grain from Western Canada because the determination of the price in Liverpool depends on the transportation charges. But if we fix the maximum charges we still find ourselves in the position that we have been in in tlie past, namely, that the transportation companies on the lakes may reduce their charges so as to meet the competitive rates for shipment to the Liverpool markets and the West will not be injured by it.
It is to be regretted that we have not before the Committee more facts on which to determine the issue in regard to the regulation of transportation rates by water. But I wish to discuss the matter on general principles. It has been said that a ship, or shipowner, does not require any franchise. If he does not require any franchise, he is that much better off. When a railway corporation gets a franchise, it is put to the expense of costly construction of railways through the length and breadth of the country but the great national highways which we have in addition to the railways are the rivers and lakes. These are highways which have been constructed by the Dominion Government. They have been dredged, canalized; they are guarded in season, they have their buoys placed in them and they have their
lighthouses erected upon them. The Government has also erected, at a cost of many millions of dollars, docks for the purposes of shipping and the charges which have been collected recently are not in any way commensurate with the service which has been rendered. They start out with that great asset without the expenditure of one single dollar on the part of the men who own the ships. Is it too much, ~ then, to ask this Government to go one step farther and say that where they have absolute jurisdiction over the railways they should have some slight jurisdiction over the boats that traverse those waters?
In the United States where there was a demand that water transportation should be reasonably checked by legislation, the same difficulties arose as had arisen in connection with land transportation. We found that they had their pernicious system o>f rebating. We found that one shipper could bid for the goods of different men at different prices and carry on an unfair competition. We found that they would not call at certain ports unless legislation was brought in to compel them to call at these ports. We found that in the United States, until 1916, in so far as inter-state commerce was concerned, they were an absolute law unto themselves and nobody except their own shipping jurisdiction had any authority to regulate them. It has been contended that it would do great harm and occasion a great hardship, to legislate in this matter.
But that is what was done in the United States. In 1916 they introduced in the United States a statute, not, as was suggested in the Committee when this matter was under discussion, as a war measure, but just simply for the purpose of regulating what might be termed a public utility, or what is known to everybody as a common carrier. There were subsequent amendments made to the Act, twice, in 1918, and these amendments were the branches of the law which particularly had reference to the war phase of it. The United States to-day controls its shipping on the Great Lakes, as well as its foreign shipping, under that statute. They have authority whereby they can fix their rates, examine agreements entered into between various companies and whereby they can compel the publication of tariffs of rates in reference to marine transportation.. Every possible evil which arose in connection with railway transportation in the United States arose in connection with water transport*-

tion, and these matters were dealt with by the Shipping Act in 1916.
What is the position with reference to the navigation companies? There can be no iques-tion that not very long ago there were a large number of these companies owning a few small boats on the rivers and lakes. But these independent companies are being absorbed very rapidly by large corporations. We find that the principal of these are the Dominion Marine Association, the Montreal Transportation Company, the Canada Steamships lines, the Great Lakes Transportation Company, the St. Lawrence and Chicago Steam Navigation Company, and the Ottawa Transportation Company.
There is being created in this country a monopoly in connection with our inland - steamship service just as a monopoly was being created in connection with our railways. Although the opposition to this amendment is so loud and so strenuous, because it is feared that the poor shippers will have to pay higher rates, no person can tell this House that when we get a combine and a monopoly of the water transportation companies, such as is growing at the present time, that combine, that monopoly, is being created for the purpose of the reduction of freight rates by water. It is said that we will lose competition, that there will be fewer boats to carry our grain from the West. But, so long as there are a hundred thousand, or a million, or a hundred million, bushels of grain to be carried from the head of the Great Lakes to Buffalo or to Montreal, just so long will there be competition among shippers to carry that grain.
A public service corporation in the form of a common carrier is just as great a public service corporation as we can have in this country, and it should be as amenable to regulation as any other public service body. We are rapidly coming to the time when it requires a great deal of money to organize these transportation bodies. When we have that money placed in them we have created a monopoly by reason of the large investment made for the purpose of carrying on its operations. And when we have such a monopoly in public service work the Government should step in and either take it over or exercise jurisdiction for control of its operations.
It seems to me that there is nothing unreasonable in the amendment, and that this Government could well take a step in a forward direction by at least adopting the amendment and proceeding to establish

maximum rates of transportation charges imposed by these corporations.

I am going to support the amendment. In British Columbia we have a coastal service which is practically monopolized by the Union Steamship Company, and that company is taking advantage of ithe situation to discriminate against certain ports of call. I am informed that at one place called Gibson's Landing, which is about thirty miles from Vancouver, some of the residents had a misunderstanding with this company, and by way of retaliation the company cut out the call there. Now, if we had a regulating body for these steamship companies it would be impossible for them to discriminate in that manner. It seems to me that there can be no real objection to the Board of Railway Commissioners having jurisdiction over steamboat companies as well as over railway companies. If railway regulation has proved to be satisfactory-and I think every one admits that that is the case- then why should not similar regulation be satisfactory in the case of water transportation? I am in favour of this resolution.

Several years ago the
Council of Agriculture, on behalf of organized agriculture in the West, made representations to the Federal Government to have lake transportation regulated, and I am sorry to-night, Mr. Chairman, to see the Minister of Railways objecting to this amendment. It is a progressive movement, but our Minister of Railways sees fit to support private corporations-he sees fit to support a large monopoly, for that is what I understand the Canadian Steamship Company to be, and naturally those interested in it very much resent being brought under proper control. As the hon. member for East Lambton stated, he is not asking that the rates be controlled exactly, but that a maximum rate be set; and if steamship companies choose to carry freight at a lower rate than the maximum by all means let them do so means let them do so.
I was very glad to hear that Mr. Car-ruthers when he discovered what kind of a company he was in-this Canada Steamship Company-pulled out to save himself.
The effect of the excessive rates charged on the lakes for the transportation of our wheat to the seaboard has a very adverse effect on business, for it tends to stagnation, and in fact sometimes causes a blockade. When the transaction of selling wheat at Port Arthur takes place the exporter, not knowing the rates he will have to pay

when his grain is shipped out, naturally charges the highest rate that has been in existence, and to make himself absolutely sure he charges a higher rate than what he would need to do if the rates were fixed. Thus this excessive rate which he is obliged to charge affects the producer and also the consumer, and thereby tends to stagnate trade. The wheat is held up in the elevators, which very often are filled to capacity, and all the available box cars are resorted to for storage, and the initial elevators are also congested, simply because the exporter has no guarantee as to the rate he will have to pay on exporting the grain. Not only does it affect the producer of the grain, but it also affects every business man in the country. It is a well known fact that if the farmer cannot sell his produce he cannot pay his debts to the business man, and if the business man does not get his money from the farmer how can he continue in business?
I hope to see this amendment carried. This is not a party government any more, we do not need to wonder what will the party think; what we need to be concerned about is what will the people think of this progressive movement? The hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Robb), I think, was very anxious lest the westerners freeze in the winter time, and he wanted to see them get their coal supply as cheaply as possible. I venture to say that if the rates were under control, those of us in the West who do use coal brought up to Port Arthur by boat would at least get it as cheap or cheaper than we do today.
The hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Stewart) remarked that the steamships on the lakes get no benefit from the Government. I think he did not mean to say that, because he surely knows that any ship plying on the lakes of Canada has the benefit of the aids to navigation provided by the Government, As has been stated by the hon. member for East Lambton, when the proposed extensions and improvements to navigation are completed they will have [DOT]cost this country over $400,000,000. That enormous expenditure is for the deepening of channels and the construction of canals and locks, and our steamships plying on the lakes will have the benefit and the free use of those aids to navigation. Yet they say:	We get no help from the Government; therefore our rates should not be brought under the control of the State.
This matter affects one of the most important links in our transportation system. We are approaching the time when we shall
be up against the keenest competition on the wheat market at Liverpool that we have ever seen. The countries of the world that were producing wheat in the past will again turn to that production, and Western Canadian wheat must be subjected to such a very 'long haul both by rail and by water, that if the rates are not cut down to an equitable basis we shall not be able to compete with our wheat on the markets of the world. The Committee should be very careful in considering this proposed amendment; the matter is of vital importance not only to the farmers of Western Canada and to the businessmen .as well, but to the Dominion as a whole. It is our surplus products that will eventually pay our huge debt.

There have been one or two statements in connection with this discussion which, I think, in the interests of the people should be cleared up in the minds of a few hon. members. I do not think it necessary to clear them up in the minds of business men, because I do not know of any Board of Trade, any shipper, any elevator man, any grain man, or any man who is interested in the .shipping of the country in a practical way and has an accurate knowledge of shipping conditions in Canada, who has either made a complaint or expressed a desire for this legislation. Therefore it is only fair to say to my hon. friend (Mr. J. F. Reid) that there are one or two facts which the people to whom I have referred know much better than I do, and which I think it is proper to present for his consideration. One of them is this. The price of the wheat of the world is fixed at Liverpool. All wheat meets there, whether it comes from the Argentine, from Canada, or from the United States. Wheat from the Canadian West has to go to Liverpool, and it is in the public interest that it get there as cheaply as possible. There are two routes which it can take: via Buffalo and New York, or via Port Colborne and Montreal. That is the first competition that is presented to every shipping company that is not controlled by a railroad corporation; and they have to beat that Buffalo-New York route if they are to ship via Montreal. Let me tell you why. The rate of freight from New York to Liverpool has always determined the rate from Montreal to Liverpool. To meet that rate the Canadian boats, have to beat the Buffalo-New York rate; they have to get to Montreal cheaper if they are to pay the addi-

We have reached the time in the history of Canada when public utilities are in a large measure coming

under public supervision or control. So far as I can see, no valid reason has been presented to-night for not bringing shipping rates under control of the Railway Commission. Years ago it was found absolutely necessary in the interest of transportation to bring railway rates under the control of the Federal Government. Every argument that has been used here to-night against the bringing of the shipping interests under the control of the Government was used at that time against the bringing of the railways under that control. We have had years .of experience with railways under government control through the board that is now operating, and we have no complaint against that control. Everybody is of the opinion, I believe, that it was a good thing in the interest of Canada that transportation by rail was brought under the supervision of the Railway Board.
How much more does it cost to carry a bushel of grain from Fort William to Montreal than it did three years ago?

When I am through, the hon. member may ask his question. I want to present my argument and the hon. member has had an opportunity of presenting his. Every argument that was used in favour of bringing the railways under the jurisdiction of the Railway Board might be and has been reasonably put forward to-night why we should bring the shipping interests under some similar control. Now that we have tested out the value of control by the Railway Board, I believe we are quite safe in asking also that our water transportation mediums might be brought under similar control.
A great deal has been said to-night about fixing rates, and it was said that by fixing rates you preclude shipping companies from any right they might wish to exercise of carrying goods at a lower rate than the rate fixed. If it was a fixed rate, then the argument would hold good, but when it is not a fixed rate, but a maximum rate we are asking for, there is no argument in the statement. Ships can lower their rates as much as they see fit; all we ask is that there be a maximum rate beyond which they cannot go. Therefore, all that has been said along the line of interfering with railways reducing rates in order to get business, does not obtain here at all, and there is no argument in it.
Four years ago this matter came under consideration in the West. The interests
represented by the producers of one of the most important commodities we have to ship in this country gave careful consideration to this question at the time. They passed resolutions urging that the Government of Canada should bring Canadian shipping interests under the control of some board, and a request made by a large producing interest like that should have consideration. There are two classes of people affected directly by the control of rates; one is the producer and the other is the consumer. I claim that the producing interests of Canada are practically a unit in asking for the fixing of a maximum rate. I claim further that the great consuming interests of Canada are largely behind those asking for the fixing of a maximum rate. The resolutions that have come here have come from boards of trade, from manufacturing associations and from wholesalers. These are people occupying a middle position, and it matters vety little to them what attitude they take as regards fixing of rates. It affects them very little whether the rate is increased or not, because all they have to do is to add the increase to the cost of the goods and pass it on to the consumer. Both the producer and the consumer who are affected by the fixing of rates are largely if not entirely in favour of the amendment, and 1 therefore desire to urge as strongly as I can upon the Government the imports anee of giving careful consideration to this amendment. If the Government vote against this amendment, this will be another case where the statement may toe made that the high cost of living is not being dealt with sympathetically by them.
Mr. G. B. NICHOLsON: The hon. member for Toronto Centre( Mr. Bristol) put his finger on the pulse of the situation as regards the steamship companies when he said that what they wished to maintain was a flexibility in rates. If that is interpreted in another way, it means that the steamship companies wish to be in a position which will enable them to discriminate between shippers and to quote to shippers that are within the circle a rate that they will not give to those who are without. It just narrows the water-borne traffic situation down to this, that no man in business anywhere in Canada to-day can undertake to enter into a contract for the delivery of a commodity anywhere in Canada if it has to be transported by water, and know that he is going to get transportation at all or that he is going to get it within a certain radii of rates, because at the time

the goods are ready to be shipped, he is absolutely at .the mercy of the steamship companies. The hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Stewart) challenged the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) to cite an instance where discrimination had taken place or where a steamship company had failed to carry out its contract. I can cite a case where a steamship company entered into a contract to transport a large volume of freight, and because, in the interim between the time the contract was signed and the time the goods were to be transported, conditions had developed that made it possible for them to get any rate they asked, they repudiated their contract notwithstanding the fact that by so doing they placed the shipper of those goods in a position that meant ultimate bankruptcy. I know perfectly well the hon. member will say that the shipper had his recourse in the courts. That is true, and the shipper took recourse and the case has been before the courts for four years, and I anticipate that in all human probability it will be before the courts for as long a time as the steamship company can keep it there. In the meantime what about the goods that have to be transported? The situation in connection with the transportation on the Upper Lakes narrows down to this, to say nothing of rates, that the shipper is at the mercy of one or two large transportation companies that will take his freight if it suits them to take it and that will leave it on the docks if it does not suit them to take it, and there is no possible means by which the shipper can get redress.
After we have spent $400,000,000 in developing a waterway for the transportation of the commerce of this country, and large sums to protect that waterway for the steamers, it is only fair to the shippers that there should be some control over the rates in order that the steamship 'companies should not be permitted to do just as they like. I do not intend to enter into the question of the profits that have been made, but anybody who knows conditions on the Great Lakes knows that there has been a tremendous increase in the rates on the Upper Lakes from 1914 onwards. We hear a great deal about the increase of thirty-five to forty per cent in railway rates, but I know instances where there was an increase in water rates of 200 per cent on a certain commodity within four or five months during 1915-1(5. I cannot see any logical reason why the amendment of the hon. member for East Lambton should not carry. I am not sufficiently expert to know whether

all the details are as they should be, but the principle involved is simply this: That we have as much right to control waterborne traffic as we have to control railway traffic, and I have no doubt whatever that the Railway Commission could work out the details so as to do justice to all concerned.
Amendment (Mr. J. E. Armstrong) negatived; yeas 36, nays 61.
